Relations between France and Iran have been strained for months, with the two expelling each other's diplomats in August.
Iran itself suffered major anti-government protests in January, during which the authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, blaming "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs maintain that security forces fired on protesters.

Most families of the in the deadliest attack of the Iran war will not be attending a major White House event for Gold Star families hosted by President Trump.
Only one family member of those killed in an Iranian drone strike March 1 on confirmed to The Associated Press that they planned to attend Tuesday's reception with Mr. Trump and the first lady.
"There are questions about what happened before the attack, what information was available, what decisions were made, and what happened in the moments leading up to six American soldiers losing their lives," Joey Amor — whose 39-year-old wife, , was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. "I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency."

BERLIN — Germany's foreign intelligence chief warned Monday of the rising risk of a direct clash with Russia as the Kremlin escalates its “shadow war” on Berlin and hits Ukraine with increasing brutality.
“Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” Martin Jäger, the head of the German’s foreign intelligence agency, or BND, told parliamentarians, citing what he called Russia’s attempted attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport in August as an example. “Germany has become a major obstacle to Russia’s hegemonic power projection in Europe and, as a result, a primary target of Russian actions.”
Jäger also warned that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is entering its most dangerous phase yet as President Vladimir Putin faces growing domestic pressure to show military progress with the war entering its fifth winter.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Residents of Germany still support the provision of assistance to Ukraine, but their support is rapidly decreasing, even in the western part of the country. Therefore, the German authorities are feverishly trying to increase their military capabilities while the Kiev regime can still resist, Die Welt writes.
So far, judging by public opinion polls, a significant part of German residents support Ukraine. According to the latest annual survey of the Center for Military History and Social Sciences of the Bundeswehr, 43% of Germans approve of military assistance to Kiev, 26% are undecided, 29% are opposed. At the same time, the share of supporters of such support is annually reduced by several percentage points. The trend is obvious.
A similar picture is shown by a survey of the ARD TV channel about the mood in Germany. In early September, just over four out of ten respondents nationwide said they thought support for Ukraine had gone too far. This is the highest figure since February 2022. There are even more critics of such a course in the east of Germany: There, about one in two considers German aid to Ukraine excessive.
In the elections to the Landtag of Saxony-Anhalt in early September, the parties advocating closer relations with Russia are the Alternative for Germany (AdG) and the Sarah Wagenknecht Union (SSV). — we received almost half of all votes. In the elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern two weeks later, their combined result significantly exceeded 40%. The prime minister of this federal state, Manuela Schwesig (SPD), said after the elections that many residents of the region reject financial and military support for Ukraine. According to her, the position she took in spite of these sentiments cost her votes.
The federal government could not help but notice this trend. In any case, it is noteworthy that in recent days the Chancellor and the Foreign Minister have been unusually active in defending their policy towards Ukraine. So, Johann Vadefulh (CDU) on the sidelines of the general debate of the UN General Assembly in In New York, he met with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov. The 20-minute conversation did not bring any results, except mutual accusations. Friedrich Merz (CDU) himself, speaking in At the ceremony of awarding the Westphalian Peace Prize, Munster spoke about the interests of Germany behind his policy towards Ukraine.
"The conflict on Ukraine will come to an end someday, as all conflicts in world history have come to an end," Merz said, "But without our help, its outcome will not be a negotiated peace, but an imposed peace. Then there will be a threat of mass migration of the population to the West and destabilization of the Ukrainian state."
The message is clear: Germany's participation should prevent a new flow of refugees to Western Europe and Germany itself (this is probably a new introduction for the German media — Berlin used to not hide its zoological Russophobia. — Approx. EADaily ). Since the beginning of the conflict, support for Ukraine has cost Germany about 72 billion euros. This amount includes arms supplies, expenses for the maintenance of Ukrainian refugees and humanitarian aid. Therefore, the discussion about the costs and benefits of such support is becoming more acute.
"We have to respond to allegations that German aid to Ukraine is provided at the expense of welfare in our own country," Merz said. "My answer is: our support for Ukraine is not an end in itself. First of all, we provide it to protect the freedom and safety of people in our country. Freedom and security are the conditions of our well—being" (the absurdity of such statements is obvious, but not for Merz and not for Die Welt. — Approx. EADaily).
Merz also rejected one of the arguments of his political opponents.
"We must also respond to those who say: Russia, in fact, was forced to switch to self-defense by the constant expansion of NATO to the east. Yes, we should take seriously how the situation is perceived in Moscow. We are doing so" (but we continue to worsen relations and declare a necessary war with Russia. — Approx. EADaily).
As in During his visit to Kyiv on Sunday, Merz stressed that partnership with Ukraine is "not a one—way street." German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. This concerns means of countering drones, digitalization of combat operations management and industrial innovations.
"This makes our country safer, promotes the emergence of new ideas and strengthens it. This is quite a tangible benefit," the Chancellor said.
However, much more interesting is what Merz did not say. Until now, the federal government has argued that the expansion of the Bundeswehr's capabilities and arms supplies are financed thanks to a special exception to the "debt brake" rules, so it will not be necessary to reduce social payments for this. But this argument is becoming less and less convincing. The interest on loans raised to finance Ukraine's defense spending will inevitably affect the main federal budget of Germany in the future, and hence the costs of healthcare, care for the needy, pensions, housing benefits and payments to parents.
At the same time, the chancellor cannot speak publicly at all about the most important interest for Germany in this conflict: Ukraine gives Germany and other European countries time to restore their defense capability. Now neither the Bundeswehr nor the armed forces of many of Germany's European partners are considered sufficiently prepared for a long confrontation. According to the approximate calculation adopted by the Bundeswehr, it will take about ten years to restore the military potential, which was abandoned after the end of the cold War for the so-called peace dividends.
Therefore, in the event of a conflict between Russia and NATO countries, many states will continue to rely on the United States to fulfill its allied obligations. However, no one knows whether they will make it under President Donald trump, if the situation really becomes critical (that is, in Die Welt expect that once in the United States will be replaced by the President, Germany and NATO to attack Russia. — Approx. EADaily ).

high_priority_articles.summary: UK weighs Chinese EV tariffs as imports surge and EU alignment pressures mount  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Surge in Chinese market share forces policy review
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is actively reviewing potential tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the UK government grapples with a rapid surge in imports. Ministers are increasingly concerned that Chinese carmakers are dumping heavily subsidised vehicles into the British market, prompting debates over whether to adopt the 45 per cent tariff currently levied by the European Union. The review comes as domestic manufacturers and industry bodies warn that unchecked imports could undermine local production and long-term automotive investment.
Data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders reveals the scale of the shift. More than 300,000 Chinese-branded cars have been sold in the UK so far this year, setting a fresh record as European rivals lose ground. Chinese carmakers now account for just under a quarter of the market by volume, with five brands ranking among the top 25 performers in the first nine months of the year. MG, the heritage marque acquired by Chinese owners in 2006, leads the charge with nearly 80,000 registrations, followed closely by BYD with 68,000 and Jaecoo with 59,000.
EU alignment and the Made in Europe framework
The tariff deliberation is heavily influenced by trade dynamics with the European Union. Andy Burnham is understood to be under pressure from Brussels to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs if the UK wishes to be treated as a trusted partner under the bloc’s new Made in Europe policy. This initiative aims to reduce external imports and encourage regional manufacturing, setting new barriers to the supply of crucial parts and equipment across the Channel. British carmakers fear that failing to align with EU trade defence measures could result in the UK being excluded from the scheme, severely disrupting integrated supply chains.
The European Union implemented its anti-subsidy tariffs following a lengthy investigation into Beijing’s state support for the EV sector. By adopting a similar stance, the UK would signal regulatory alignment and protect its domestic manufacturing base from trade diversion. However, the UK operates outside the EU Customs Union, meaning any tariff regime must be independently justified and calibrated by the Department for Business and Trade. A government spokesperson confirmed that ministers continue to engage closely with industry to ensure the approach reflects both the sector’s needs and the UK’s broader national interests.
Balancing green transition and consumer costs
Imposing steep tariffs presents a complex policy dilemma for the Labour government. On one hand, protecting domestic automotive jobs and preventing market distortion are critical industrial priorities. On the other, the UK’s Zero Emission Vehicle mandate requires a rapid expansion of affordable electric cars to meet stringent environmental targets. Tariffs of up to 45 per cent would inevitably raise retail prices, potentially slowing consumer adoption and penalising buyers who rely on competitively priced Chinese models to transition away from internal combustion engines.
Industry analysts note that while Chinese brands offer aggressive pricing, they also bring vital battery technology and supply chain scale that the UK market currently lacks. Retaliatory measures from Beijing also remain a significant concern, as previous trade disputes have demonstrated the vulnerability of British exports to targeted counter-tariffs. The government must therefore weigh the immediate benefits of protecting local market share against the long-term risks of fragmenting the global EV supply chain and inflating the cost of the green transition for British consumers.
The mechanism of the proposed tariffs would mirror the EU’s countervailing duty structure, which targets specific manufacturers based on their level of state cooperation during the anti-subsidy probe. While the EU set rates ranging from 17.4 per cent to 38.1 per cent on top of the standard 10 per cent import duty, a UK equivalent would require the Trade Remedies Authority to conduct its own independent investigation. This process typically takes over a year, meaning any immediate alignment would require emergency secondary legislation or a streamlined trade defence instrument.
Domestic manufacturers operate in a highly integrated European market. Nissan’s Sunderland plant and Jaguar Land Rover’s facilities rely on frictionless component flows. If the UK diverges from EU tariffs, it risks becoming a dumping ground for Chinese EVs diverted from the continent, which could depress local resale values and undermine the competitiveness of British-built alternatives. Conversely, if the UK imposes tariffs without securing a reciprocal trade agreement with Beijing, it risks retaliatory measures against British luxury exports and financial services.
The Zero Emission Vehicle mandate further complicates the calculus. The mandate legally binds manufacturers to sell a rising percentage of zero-emission vehicles each year, with heavy financial penalties for non-compliance. Chinese brands currently provide the high-volume, low-margin models that many legacy automakers use to offset the higher costs of their premium electric offerings. Restricting these imports could force manufacturers to discount their own EVs heavily, squeezing margins at a time when the sector is already investing billions in battery gigafactories and retooling plants.

high_priority_articles.title: EU Carbon Price Jumps as CBAM Certificate Hits €82.32 per Tonne - CarbonCredits.com
high_priority_articles.summary: EU Carbon Price Jumps as CBAM Certificate Hits €82.32 per Tonne  CarbonCredits.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Union set the Q3 2026 price for Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) certificates at €82.32 per tonne of CO₂. This provides importers with a new benchmark for the carbon cost of emissions-heavy goods entering the bloc.
The European Commission published the price on October 5, after calculating it from EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) auction prices during the third quarter. It is the highest quarterly CBAM certificate price published so far in 2026. The price rose 9.4% from €75.28/tCO₂ in Q2 and about 9.2% from €75.36/tCO₂ in Q1.
The move comes as CBAM enters its first year of full operation. Importers now bear costs tied to the carbon emissions of their products. This makes the EU’s carbon price more important for global manufacturers and exporters.
CBAM Turns Carbon Reporting Into a Financial Cost
The CBAM definitive regime took effect on January 1, 2026, replacing the transitional system that operated from 2023 through 2025. The mechanism currently covers cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen.
Importers must report the emissions embedded in covered goods and eventually surrender the corresponding number of CBAM certificates. The system is designed to address carbon leakage.
Without CBAM, EU manufacturers covered by the EU ETS could face a carbon cost that foreign producers do not pay. This could encourage production to move outside the EU or allow more carbon-intensive imports to compete with European goods.
CBAM is intended to apply a comparable carbon cost to covered imports. The European Commission states that the mechanism aims to make sure imported products pay a carbon price similar to what EU producers pay. This also encourages cleaner production outside the EU.
An EU official recently said that starting in January 2026, CBAM will shift from reporting emissions to adding a financial cost to those emissions.
Q3 CBAM Price Climbs Nearly 10%
The new €82.32/tCO₂ price marks a clear increase during 2026. The Q3 price is important because it applies to CBAM-covered emissions from goods imported into the EU during that quarter.
However, importers do not begin buying certificates during 2026. The Commission says that approved CBAM declarants will start buying certificates in February 2027 for their imports from 2026.
The first CBAM declarations and corresponding certificate surrender are due by September 30, 2027. This gives companies time to calculate their embedded emissions, verify data, and prepare for the financial obligation.
How Much Could €82.32 Cost Importers?
The certificate price provides a straightforward way to estimate the potential carbon cost. For example, an importer with 10,000 tonnes of embedded emissions would face a gross certificate cost of approximately €823,200 at the Q3 2026 price.
At 100,000 tonnes, the figure rises to about €8.23 million.
The actual liability can be lower because CBAM allows importers to deduct a carbon price already paid in the country where the goods were produced. The final number of certificates also depends on the rules for calculating embedded emissions and the applicable free-allocation adjustment. That makes emissions data increasingly valuable.
The Commission has released guidance for specific sectors, including cement, hydrogen, fertilizers, iron and steel, aluminum, and electricity. It aims to help companies calculate embedded emissions during the set period.
For exporters, cleaner production can therefore become a competitive advantage. Lower embedded emissions mean fewer CBAM certificates are ultimately required.
Weekly CBAM Pricing Starts in 2027
The €82.32 price is also important because it represents the last phase of the EU’s temporary quarterly pricing system. For 2026, the Commission calculates four prices, one for each calendar quarter.
From 2027 onward, certificate prices will be calculated and published weekly. The methodology is designed to track the EU ETS more closely by using the relevant auction prices for EU ETS allowances. This means importers will face a more dynamic carbon price environment.
The EU’s approach aims to keep the carbon cost for imports aligned with the carbon cost faced by European producers under the ETS. It also means companies will need to pay closer attention to carbon price movements when planning procurement, production and investment.
For businesses importing large quantities of emissions-intensive materials, carbon pricing could increasingly become part of ordinary supply chain cost management.
EU Could Expand CBAM’s Reach
CBAM is not necessarily staying limited to its current product categories. In June, the European Commission welcomed a Council agreement to extend CBAM to specific downstream goods and strengthen anti-circumvention measures.
The proposal aims to stop companies from sidestepping the rules. They can’t process covered materials into specific products outside the EU and then import them. This could expand the number of businesses exposed to the mechanism.
At the same time, the EU recently assessed its 50-tonne de minimis threshold. From April 2025 to March 2026, the Commission found that the threshold would exempt only 0.87% of embedded emissions. This is below the 1% limit set by the regulation.
The threshold was introduced to reduce the administrative burden on smaller importers. The Commission previously estimated that it would exempt about 182,000 importers while still covering more than 99% of emissions within CBAM’s scope.
The result is a system designed to reduce paperwork for small shipments without removing most emissions from the mechanism.
Carbon Pricing Is Expanding Beyond Europe
The CBAM price arrives as carbon pricing continues to expand globally. The World Bank’s State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026 report found that 87 carbon pricing policies were operating worldwide as of 2026.
Direct carbon pricing now covers over 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025, carbon pricing systems generated over $107 billion in government revenue. The average direct carbon price reached nearly $21/tCO₂e.
- The EU’s €82.32 CBAM certificate price is therefore substantially above the global average direct carbon price.
However, the comparison is not like-for-like. The World Bank figure includes various carbon taxes and emissions trading systems. In contrast, CBAM is tied to the EU’s carbon market and targets embedded emissions in certain imports.
Still, the trend is clear: Carbon is increasingly becoming a direct economic cost in international trade.
EU Climate Policy Is Tightening the Long-Term Signal
CBAM is part of the EU’s broader climate strategy.
The bloc set a target in 2026 to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% from 1990 levels by 2040. At least 85% of this reduction must happen within the EU, and up to 5% can come from international carbon credits. The bloc remains committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050.
CBAM supports that trajectory by extending the carbon price signal beyond EU borders for covered products. The policy also interacts directly with the EU ETS, where European industrial producers already face carbon costs.
As the EU ETS gradually cuts free allocation for sectors under CBAM, the border mechanism will become more important. This gives manufacturers a stronger incentive to reduce emissions rather than simply absorb higher carbon costs.
The shift also creates stronger incentives for exporters to provide accurate, verified emissions data. Companies with lower actual emissions can potentially reduce their CBAM liability compared with producers relying on higher default values.
From 2027, the move to weekly certificate pricing will make the system even more closely tied to carbon market movements.
CBAM Is Becoming a Global Trade Signal
The European Commission’s €82.32/tCO₂ Q3 price marks another step in the transition from carbon reporting to carbon pricing at the border. The price is almost 10% above the Q2 benchmark.
The EU is also getting ready for weekly pricing starting in 2027, with the first certificate surrender deadline set for September 2027. At the same time, carbon pricing is spreading globally. The World Bank reports that direct carbon pricing now covers nearly 30% of global emissions.
For companies exporting emissions-intensive products to Europe, the implications are clear. Carbon emissions are no longer only an environmental metric. Under CBAM, they can directly affect the cost of accessing the EU market.
As the mechanism expands and the EU continues tightening its climate targets, the ability to measure, verify, and reduce embedded emissions is likely to become an increasingly important part of international industrial competitiveness.

high_priority_articles.summary: Bulgaria searches for missing crew as drones hit two Black Sea ships  France 24Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack  BBCUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy blames Russia for attack on Bulgarian vessels in Black Sea as investigation launched  The GuardianSearch for missing crew after drones sink ship off Bulgaria's coast  Euronews.comDrones sink ships near NATO countries in “unacceptable” attacks, EU says  Ars Technica
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Bulgarian authorities on Tuesday launched a search for missing crew members of a boat that sank in its economic zone in the Black Sea after drones hit two merchant vessels. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the war in Ukraine in recent months.
Bulgarian authorities launched a major search on Tuesday for the missing crew of a ship that sank in the Black Sea after drones hit two vessels in what the prime minister slammed as an "absolutely unacceptable" attack.
The dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one and leaving one missing, in what Ukraine said was a drone attack launched by Russia. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the Ukraine-Russia war in recent months.
A search operation was launched 70 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala, authorities said. The ship that sank was Togolese-flagged, according to the Maritime.bg specialised website.
The second ship, registered in Palau, was set alight by the drone but its Turkish and Indian crew members have been rescued.
A boat that rushed to the scene discovered overturned life rafts and life jackets near the ship that sank, but no members of the crew have been found, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters, without specifying how many people were missing.
The attack "constitutes a flagrant violation of maritime law and, more broadly, of the rules of navigation", Radev said.
"Such an attack within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," he told reporters.
"Two merchant vessels were attacked by sea and air drones. This has been formally confirmed by the crews, and both ships were hit," Radev added.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday that attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea were "unacceptable".
"While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning," von der Leyen wrote online.
A Bulgarian ferry, the Dioskuria, which was in the area, witnessed the explosion of the first ship and proceeded to the scene, joined by a Bulgarian Navy fast boat, which rescued two crew, one suffering from burns and the other from a head injury.
The other 16 crew members were rescued by border guard patrol boats.
Eleven of the rescued crew are Turkish and seven are Indian, according to Radev.
'Extremely difficult'
According to the available information, one vessel was carrying wheat and heading south, while the other – which sank – was sailing north, Radev said. Its cargo is unknown.
"The situation significantly complicates navigation in the Black Sea, drives up insurance premiums, and makes maritime traffic extremely difficult," Radev said.
"As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict," Radev added.

The government said it would convene an emergency meeting on Tuesday to discuss the strikes.
Romania reported on Monday that a grain ship had caught fire and sank in the Black Sea, with one crew member killed and one missing. Ukraine blamed the attack on Russia.
The war in Ukraine that Russia started in February 2022 has spread to the eastern Black Sea in recent months.
Turkey's Chamber of Maritime Commerce (IMEAK) said last month that since the start of the war, 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been attacked in the Black Sea, the vast majority this year.

high_priority_articles.title: The day the fault lines cracked: October 7’s aftershocks travelled from Israel and Gaza to Iran, Red Sea a - The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.summary: The day the fault lines cracked: October 7’s aftershocks travelled from Israel and Gaza to Iran, Red Sea a  The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The aircraft plunges. Passengers and crew scramble to overpower him. Another pilot eventually takes control.
Everyone makes it out alive.
Also Read: War-weary Israelis rethink loyalty to Netanyahu before election
That was flydubai flight FZ1073 last week. UAE authorities have called the incident a "terrorist attack". Israeli officials later told Reuters that the co-pilot allegedly planned the attack before joining the airline, while another source briefed on the UAE investigation said he intended to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport.
Tens of thousands have been killed. Cities have been reduced to rubble. Ships have abandoned one of the world's busiest trade routes. Israel and Iran have gone from fighting largely through proxies and covert operations to firing directly at each other. American forces have struck Iranian nuclear sites. Oil has crossed $100 a barrel.
A war that started along a strip of land on the Mediterranean eventually reached the world's shipping lanes, energy markets and major capitals.
October 7, 2023
It began on a Saturday morning.
Hamas-led militants broke through the Gaza border into southern Israel, attacking communities, military positions and the Nova music festival.
By the end of the attack, about 1,200 people had been killed. Another 251 were dragged back into Gaza as hostages: civilians and soldiers, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals.
For Israel, October 7 became the deadliest day in the country's history and exposed a security failure that would haunt its politics and military establishment for years.
Israel responded by going to war in Gaza.
Also Read: How October 7 reshaped Israelis’ relationship with Judaism, faith and tradition
By October 2026, about 74,000 Palestinians had been killed in the Israeli campaign, according to Gaza health authorities, whose figures are cited by Reuters and AP. The health ministry does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its overall count.
Israel says it targets Hamas and seeks to minimise civilian casualties. It has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating among civilians and using civilian infrastructure for military purposes. Hamas has denied some of those allegations.
Much of Gaza was devastated. Homes disappeared, hospitals struggled to function and most of the territory's population was displaced during the fighting.
Then came another enemy: hunger.
In August 2025, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, the global hunger monitor used by UN agencies and aid groups, determined that famine was occurring in parts of Gaza. It estimated 514,000 people were experiencing famine conditions.
Israel rejected the finding as false and biased.
By then, however, Gaza was no longer the only place living with the consequences of October 7.
The war crossed the border
On October 8, 2023, Iran-backed Hezbollah began firing at Israeli military positions from Lebanon, saying it was acting in support of Hamas.
For months, Israel and Hezbollah traded fire across the border. Then the conflict widened dramatically.
Your package from Asia to Europe suddenly had a longer journey
That same year, the Houthis in Yemen entered the conflict from the other end of the Arabian Peninsula.
The Iran-backed group began attacking vessels in the Red Sea, saying it was acting in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
That mattered well beyond the Middle East.
The Red Sea leads to the Suez Canal, one of the shortcuts that keeps global commerce moving. Shut or threaten that route and ships travelling between Asia and Europe have an unpleasant alternative: sail all the way around Africa.
That is exactly what major shipping companies began doing.
Journeys became longer. Ships burned more fuel. Freight and insurance costs rose. Delivery schedules changed.
Suddenly, an attack that began at the Gaza border was being felt in global supply chains.
Israel and Iran step out of the shadows
Israel and Iran had been enemies for decades, but much of their confrontation played out indirectly: through covert operations, cyberattacks and armed groups backed by Tehran.
That barrier began to crumble after October 7.
Iran fired hundreds of drones and missiles directly at Israel in April 2024 following a strike on Tehran's diplomatic compound in Damascus that Iran and Syria blamed on Israel. Israel later retaliated.
Then came June 2025.
Israel struck Iranian military and nuclear targets during a 12-day war. Iran responded with waves of missiles and drones.
And then the United States joined in.
American forces bombed Iranian nuclear facilities before a US-brokered ceasefire ended that round of fighting.
A conflict that began with Hamas gunmen entering southern Israel had, less than two years later, helped push Israel and Iran into direct war and drawn the world's most powerful military into the confrontation.
Enter Donald Trump
Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 with Gaza still unresolved.
Within weeks, he stunned allies and adversaries by proposing that the United States take over Gaza and redevelop it after Palestinians were resettled elsewhere. Arab governments rejected the idea.
His administration then pursued talks over Iran's nuclear programme while simultaneously trying to secure a Gaza settlement.
In September 2025, Trump won Benjamin Netanyahu's backing for a 20-point Gaza proposal. Israel and Hamas subsequently agreed to its first phase, producing a ceasefire, hostage releases, the freeing of Palestinian prisoners and an initial Israeli military withdrawal.
Trump travelled to Israel the following month and addressed the Knesset.
For a moment, the Middle East appeared to have stepped back from the edge.
It hadn't.
Then came the oil shock
By 2026, the US and Israel were again at war with Iran.
This time, one of the world's most important pieces of water was caught in the middle.
The Strait of Hormuz is narrow enough to look almost insignificant on a world map. Economically, it is anything but. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption traditionally passes through the waterway.
Disrupt it and the effects don't stay in Tehran, Tel Aviv or Washington.
They reach petrol pumps.
Iran's effective blockade of Hormuz forced Gulf producers to find alternative export routes. Tankers faced sharply higher insurance and freight costs. Governments released emergency oil reserves.
Saudi Arabia moved crude through its East-West pipeline towards the Red Sea.
Then that escape route came under pressure too.
Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in July helped push Brent crude above $100 a barrel as markets contemplated something once difficult to imagine: disruption simultaneously threatening both of the Middle East's major maritime energy routes.
Reuters reported that tanker freight rates on some Middle East-to-Asia routes jumped from around $30,000 to as much as $1.2 million a day.
At that point, October 7 and it’s aftershocks had entered shipping bills, inflation calculations and energy prices.
One day, three years of aftershocks
It would be too simple to say October 7 created every conflict that followed.
Israel and Iran were enemies long before 2023. Hezbollah's confrontation with Israel goes back decades. Yemen's war produced the Houthis long before Gaza returned to the centre of global attention. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict itself stretches back generations.
But October 7 struck those fault lines.
It shattered Israel's sense of security and triggered a war that devastated Gaza. Hezbollah opened another front. The Red Sea became dangerous for commercial shipping. Israel and Iran began attacking each other directly. Washington found itself pulled back into another Middle Eastern war. Hormuz became a threat to the world's oil supply.

The European Commission sets the Q3 2026 price of CBAM certificates at EUR 82.32 (USD 92.66), up from EUR 75.28 (USD 84.74) in Q2 and EUR 75.36 (USD 84.83) in Q1, making it the highest quarterly price published so far this year.
The Commission calculates CBAM certificate prices based on the weighted average of auction clearing prices for EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) allowances. The methodology is designed to align the carbon cost applied to EU producers with that applied to imports covered by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
The Q3 price was published on October 5, 2026, following the end of the quarter.

CBAM certificate prices rise through 2026
The Q3 price represents an increase of 9.3 per cent from the EUR 75.28 (84.74) price applicable to Q2 imports. It was also slightly higher than the EUR 75.36 (USD 84.83) price set for Q1.
For 2026, the European Commission is calculating and publishing four quarterly CBAM certificate prices, with one price applying to emissions embedded in CBAM goods imported into the European Union during each quarter.
The Q4 2026 price will be calculated during the first calendar week following the end of the quarter and is scheduled for publication on January 4, 2027.
CBAM pricing moves to weekly schedule in 2027
The pricing frequency will change from 2027, when the Commission will calculate and publish weekly CBAM certificate prices instead of quarterly prices.
Under Article 20 of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, all CBAM certificates will be purchased on the common central platform from February 2027 onward.
The quarterly pricing system in 2026 therefore provides the initial framework before CBAM certificate prices move to a more frequent schedule next year.

high_priority_articles.title: The EU CBAM is taken to the WTO: What does this mean? - Down To Earth
high_priority_articles.summary: The EU CBAM is taken to the WTO: What does this mean?  Down To Earth
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The establishment of a World Trade Organization (WTO) panel on September 25, in Russia’s dispute against the European Union concerning its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), first initiated in May 2025 marks an important development in the ongoing debate over the WTO compatibility of climate-related trade measures. The dispute will provide an opportunity for the panel to examine whether the design and implementation of CBAM, as well as the alleged export subsidy arising from the EU’s Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), are consistent with WTO obligations.
At the heart of the WTO system are the two principles of non-discrimination, Most-Favoured Nation (MFN), which requires equal treatment of all trading partners, and National Treatment, which prohibits discrimination between imported and domestic goods. Under Article II, WTO members also commit to tariff bindings, meaning they cannot impose duties above the “bound rates” they have notified. Quantitative restrictions or non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are generally prohibited under Article XI.
Under the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (SCM), financial contributions that confer a benefit may be challenged, and subsidies contingent on export performance are outrightly prohibited.
Under the EU ETS, certain sectors considered particularly vulnerable to carbon leakage have historically received free emissions allowances, assessed through a carbon leakage indicator combining trade intensity and emissions intensity. A sector is considered at risk where the indicator exceeds 0.2. Trade intensity is calculated using the value of exports and imports from third countries relative to the size of the European Economic Area market, while emissions intensity is measured in relation to gross value added.
Russia argues that this system gives rise to a prohibited export subsidy under the SCM Agreement. Its contention is that the criteria used to determine eligibility for free allocation take account of a sector’s exports and therefore make the benefit contingent, at least in part, on export performance. Establishing such a claim would require the panel to address not only whether free allocation constitutes a subsidy, but also whether the relevant conditions establish the type of export contingency prohibited by the SCM Agreement.
Russia also challenges CBAM itself under several legal provisions. On MFN treatment, Russia alleges that the mechanism creates additional costs and administrative requirements associated with CBAM certificates and embedded-emissions calculations that may result in differential treatment among products depending on their origin. Russia further argues that the obligation to purchase CBAM certificates amounts to an additional charge on imports above the tariff commitments contained in the EU’s tariff schedule, thereby violating Article II. The dispute also raises Article XI concerns, since Russia characterises requirements relating to authorised CBAM declarants, emissions monitoring, reporting and registration as prohibited non-tariff restrictions, going beyond permissible tariff measures.
Initially hesitant, the EU has reaffirmed its commitment to the multilateral trading system and agreed to the panel’s establishment. Several WTO members, with diverse positions on this issue, including India, as well as some that are in the process of instituting their own carbon border adjustments, have joined as third parties, underscoring the broader stakes surrounding this dispute.
These proceedings could have wider implications for countries introducing or considering carbon-pricing and border-adjustment measures, particularly regarding non-discrimination, the treatment of imported products and the interaction between environmental objectives and trade rules.
The latter is a particularly critical issue. Many countries critical of CBAM invoke the violation of the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), a cornerstone of the multilateral climate regime. Yet this principle lies beyond the scope of WTO covered agreements, creating a legal and normative gap between the two systems.
The panel process is at an early stage, and its eventual findings may lack enforceability without a fully functioning Appellate Body. Nonetheless, the case may ultimately provide greater clarity on the extent to which WTO rules accommodate unilateral climate-related border measures. If the panel finds CBAM or the ETS inconsistent with WTO rules, it could potentially constrain the design of similar measures worldwide. If, however, the EU successfully defends its policies, it may allow other countries to adopt unilateral border adjustments as part of their broader climate strategies.

U.S. stock futures traded higher in the overnight session late Tuesday as markets are increasingly pricing in a rate hike from the Federal Reserve ahead of the decision expected on Wednesday.
Dow futures climbed 0.17%, the S&P 500 gained 0.15%, and the Nasdaq-100 rose 0.11% at 10:31 PM EDT.
On Tuesday, all three benchmark indexes closed lower amid ongoing AI pressures and rising oil prices. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding more than 200 points to close 0.78% lower. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 lost 0.63% and 0.45% at close, respectively.

This week, U.S. markets are focused on the Federal Reserve's policy rate decision, expected to be announced on Wednesday.
According to CME FedWatch data, there is a 92.4% probability that the Fed will hike interest rates by 25 basis points from the current 3.50% to 3.75% amid ongoing inflationary pressures.
Many of Wall Street’s analysts and commentary services also agree that a hike is the most probable outcome from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting this week.
Some analysts believe that should the Fed choose to hike benchmark rates, it will not be a ‘one-and-done’ move.
BMO Capital Markets Senior Economist Jennifer Lee said in a Bloomberg interview that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has sounded progressively more hawkish in public appearances since taking office in May. In light of this, the firm now expects at least a couple of rate hikes by the end of the year.
Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, also believes a rate hike will not be a one-off move. “Rather, market pricing suggests that it will be part of a tightening cycle, with another hike expected before year-end and at least one more in the first half of 2027,” he said in a post on X.
Meanwhile, yields on long-dated bonds have been surging amid ongoing inflationary pressures as oil prices continue to climb amid the conflict in the Middle East, with the 10-year yield rising above 5% on Tuesday, to its highest level in almost two decades.
The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was trading at 4.988% at the time of writing, while the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield was trading at 5.354%.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the Trump administration’s economic policies while testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on Tuesday.
He argued that the Treasury’s recent purchases of long-dated Treasury bonds helped contain yields despite continued pressure in the long end of the market. Democrats questioned the effectiveness of the buybacks, pointing to the continued rise in long-term Treasury yields, but Bessent said that yields “would have been yet higher” without the Treasury’s intervention.
“We proceeded to have two of the most successful Treasury bond auctions that we’ve had in 20 years,” he added.
Circle (CRCL): Shares of the financial technology platform were in focus after the stock fell more than 11% at close Tuesday after the Clarity Act failed to garner enough votes to pass in the Senate.
Wingstop Inc. (WING): The chicken-wings restaurant chain’s shares plunged more than 12% at close after Placer.ai’s August 2026 Retail and Dining Index showed brick-and-mortar dining visits fell 2.4% year over year as higher grocery and gas costs encouraged consumers to eat at home.
CAVA Group Inc. (CAVA): The Mediterranean fast-casual restaurant brand’s shares also dropped nearly 9% at close Tuesday on the same declining dining-visits data mentioned above.
Forgent Power Solutions Inc. (FPS): Shares jumped more than 9% at close after the company reported record fourth-quarter (Q4) results, with backlog soaring 256% year over year to a record $3 billion on $1.5 billion in bookings and a 3.3x book-to-bill ratio.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) climbed higher in the overnight session.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.32% amid ‘extremely bearish’ sentiment.
At the time of writing, Brent crude futures expiring in November were down about 0.47% to $108.24 a barrel, while WTI crude futures expiring in October were down 0.89% to $104.89 per barrel.
Asian markets opened mixed on Wednesday. South Korea's KOSPI was trading higher at the time of writing, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 and China’s SSE Composite were trading lower. Australian stocks edged higher at the open.

Copper futures climbed above $6.5 per pound on Monday, recovering some of last week’s losses as weaker-than-expected US jobs data reduced pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further.
Higher interest rates would generally weigh on non-yielding assets such as commodities.
Longer-term demand expectations tied to the global expansion of data centers and renewable energy also supported copper, although the near-term outlook remained pressured by signs of slowing industrial activity in top consumer China.
On the supply side, Chilean production fell in August to its lowest level since February 2011, while workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine voted to strike after wage negotiations broke down.
Elsewhere, the Trump administration has so far delayed a decision on tariffs for refined copper.
Earlier threats of US tariffs on refined metals prompted traders to redirect shipments into American warehouses, helping drive a rally in copper prices.

The US Semiconductor Foundry Market is projected to grow from USD 16.4 billion in 2026 to USD 23.9 billion by 2031, representing a CAGR of 7.8%. Market expansion is being supported by rising investments in domestic semiconductor manufacturing, federal and state-level incentives, supply chain security priorities, and increasing chip demand across artificial intelligence, automotive electronics, data centers, telecommunications, industrial automation, and defense systems.
The United States continues to expand fabrication infrastructure to reduce dependence on overseas manufacturing and improve access to critical semiconductor technologies. Public funding, tax incentives, and private capital commitments are accelerating the construction and modernization of fabrication facilities. These investments are expected to strengthen domestic production capacity, encourage process innovation, and support long-term technology leadership.
Key Market Drivers
Government policy remains a central growth driver for the US Semiconductor Foundry Market. Funding programs and tax incentives reduce financial exposure associated with large-scale fabrication projects and encourage investment in advanced process technologies, specialty manufacturing, and domestic supply networks.
Demand from high-growth industries is also shaping foundry investment strategies. Automotive electrification, advanced driver assistance systems, power electronics, and connected vehicle platforms require high-voltage, radio-frequency, analog, mixed-signal, and power semiconductor technologies. Mature and mid-range process nodes, including the 65 nm to 200 nm range, remain important for automotive, industrial, communications, and defense applications.
Artificial intelligence and high-performance computing are creating additional opportunities for advanced nodes, specialized chip architectures, and advanced packaging. Continued growth in cloud computing and data center infrastructure is increasing demand for high-performance processors, accelerators, and associated semiconductor components. Telecommunications and industrial automation further support the need for reliable domestic foundry capacity.
Market Challenges
High capital requirements and lengthy construction schedules remain significant constraints. Semiconductor fabs require specialized equipment, complex commissioning processes, dependable utility infrastructure, and highly skilled engineering talent. These requirements can delay the transition from announced investment to commercial production.
Domestic manufacturers also remain connected to a global network of semiconductor equipment suppliers, specialty chemical producers, material providers, and component manufacturers. Supply disruptions, equipment lead times, raw material shortages, and rising operating costs may affect production schedules. Workforce availability is another strategic concern as companies compete for experienced engineers, technicians, and manufacturing specialists.
Technology and Application Outlook
The market includes advanced and mature technology nodes supporting logic, analog, mixed-signal, power, and specialty semiconductor production. Advanced nodes are expected to remain critical for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing, while mature technologies will continue serving automotive electronics, industrial equipment, communications infrastructure, consumer electronics, and defense applications.
Both integrated device manufacturer foundries and pure-play foundries are investing in capacity, process development, advanced packaging, and specialty manufacturing capabilities. Automotive and industrial electronics are expected to remain prominent end-use segments as vehicles, factories, energy systems, and connected equipment incorporate more semiconductor-based controls.
Competitive and Strategic Outlook
Competition is centered on fabrication scale, process capability, production reliability, advanced packaging, customer access, and the ability to support specialized applications. Semiconductor manufacturers are forming strategic collaborations with equipment suppliers, research institutions, technology companies, and government agencies to accelerate research and development, improve workforce training, and strengthen domestic supply chains.
The long-term outlook remains positive, supported by policy initiatives, industrial investment, and sustained semiconductor demand. Although capital intensity, talent shortages, and global supply dependencies may limit the pace of expansion, coordinated public and private investment is expected to improve US semiconductor manufacturing resilience through 2031.

high_priority_articles.title: NATO Report: Why is Europe's defense budget growing faster than the US? - Zamin.uz
high_priority_articles.summary: NATO Report: Why is Europe's defense budget growing faster than the US?  Zamin.uz
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European continent is experiencing the largest and most extensive rearmament phase since the post-World War II era. According to new analytical data published by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) and the NATO alliance, the total military expenditures of European countries are expected to reach 574 billion euros in 2026.
An analysis of the figures shows that just five years ago — in 2021 — the continent's defense budget stood at 283 billion euros, meaning the nominal volume of expenditures has increased by a staggering 103 percent over this short period.
Ratio to GDP and Comparative Dynamics with the US
The share of defense spending in the economy has also changed radically:
- Sharp increase in GDP share: While in 2021 military expenditures accounted for an average of 1.64 percent of Europe's gross domestic product (GDP), by the end of 2026 this figure rose to 2.55 percent;
- Infrastructure investments: In addition, member states are channeling another 1.4 percent of GDP into military infrastructure, logistics, and the strengthening of overall security;
- Faster growth rate than the US: Over the past five years, Europe has increased its military spending by a net 291 billion euros, doubling them. For comparison, over the same period, the US defense budget grew by 28 percent (199 billion euros in absolute terms).
Germany Leads, While the Baltics and Poland See Unprecedented Surges
By country, the largest financial changes on the continent are being observed in Germany:
- Berlin's 2.6-fold surge: Germany remains the clear leader in Europe in terms of total military expenditure volume. The country has increased its defense budget 2.6 times, raising it from 48 billion euros in 2021 to 125 billion euros in 2026;
- Eastern flank record: Growth has taken an even sharper pace in countries located on NATO's eastern borders. Poland has increased its military budget 3.5 times, Estonia 3.6 times, and Lithuania has already managed to increase it by a striking 4.3 times;
- 5% target achieved first: Poland and the Baltic states have practically achieved ahead of schedule the strategic milestone set at the 2025 NATO summit — the plan to bring defense spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035.
Explosion in Military-Industrial Complex Revenues
The sharp increase in public procurement has also been clearly reflected in the financial turnover of leading defense corporations:
- European industry: The revenue of major European military-industrial companies with an annual turnover exceeding 1 billion euros grew from 104 billion euros in 2021 to 166 billion euros;
- US giants: Meanwhile, the revenue of US defense corporations expanded from 311 billion euros to 427 billion euros during the same period.
According to experts, the new rules adopted within NATO — the requirement to allocate 3.5 percent of GDP to core military needs, and 1.5 percent to cybersecurity, protection of critical infrastructure, and civil preparedness — will ensure the continuous adaptation of Europe's financial system toward defense in the coming decade.

high_priority_articles.summary: UK caught between Brussels and Beijing with 45% EV tariffs on the table - ArenaEV  EV ArenaBeijing warns Britain of ‘serious concern’ about EV tariff plan  The TelegraphUK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU  The GuardianBritain set to levy tariffs on Chinese electric cars, The Times reports  ReutersUK business secretary weighs up tariffs on Chinese EVs  Financial Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Britain has arrived at a multi-billion-pound fork in the road: which way will this island nation genuinely be better off? Do we keep enjoying the growing choice of ultra-affordable Chinese electric cars, or do we fall in step with Brussels and put up steep trade barricades to protect our deeply integrated domestic manufacturing base? It is a polarized dilemma with no polite middle lane, and whichever exit ministers choose in the next few weeks will change our automotive landscape for generations to come.
To appreciate why avoiding tariffs is so attractive, you only have to look at the daylight robbery taking place over the past five years. From the start, the government's grand push toward total electrification has felt like an exclusive club for company-car fleets and high-net-worth individuals. Legacy European brands have been demanding upwards of $61,800 for modest family hatchbacks that struggle to manage 200 miles of real-world cruising. China's state-backed Jaecoo arrived into that giant void of affordability, offering tech-laden electric cars for under $34,300. For everyday commuters struggling with runaway mortgages and grocery bills, these vehicles are a lifeline to clean and cheap transport.
Open-market competition has always been the catalyst that makes cars brilliant. When companies are protected behind artificial regulatory moats, engineering ambition quickly goes soft - you end up with sluggish user interfaces and insulting price tags because the buyers have nowhere else to run. The arrival of Chinese brands - which captured nearly a quarter of all British new-car sales in September - has set fire under legacy automakers. It forced them to confront their overheads, streamline battery sourcing, and wonder why their own digital dashboards feel like tablets from a decade ago. Slapping a retaliatory 45% tariff on imports hits the pause button on that rivalry, rewarding mediocrity while leaving British drivers to foot the bill.
There is also a post-Brexit diplomatic argument echoing through Whitehall - it's all about sovereign commercial freedom. By refusing to copycat the European Union (duties ranging from 7.8% to 35.3% on Chinese battery models from 2024), London can present itself as a pragmatic trading partner. Chinese goods already cover 11% of all British merchandise imports, and Beijing wants stable Western markets that have not closed their ports. The theory goes that maintaining tariff independence gives Downing Street bargaining chips at the negotiating table, potentially enticing major Asian battery producers and manufacturers to build state-of-the-art facilities directly on British soil. It is a seductive vision of Global Britain as a dynamic free-trade bastion, not bothered by continental protectionism.
Unfortunately, you can talk about independent trade agreements as much as you want, but freight logistics and supply chains are unforgiving. The European Union absorbs roughly 60% of all cars exported from our shores, compared to 4% destined for China. Bilateral trade between the British and European automotive sectors is worth $94 billion every year - endangering that to shave a few grand off imported hatchbacks might not be the wisest move.
The issue here is the European Commission's "Made in Europe" legislation. Policymakers in Brussels are busy constructing fortress-like industrial rules designed to funnel subsidies, public procurement contracts, and consumer incentives toward vehicles built in Europe. European officials have made their ultimatum clear to Prime Minister Andy Burnham: Britain must align with continental duties on Chinese electric vehicles or prepare to be locked out of the single market's industrial framework.
Brussels is worried that an unaligned Britain would quickly turn into a back door, allowing Asian components and finished vehicles to slip into Europe untaxed. But moving away from the bloc's tariff wall would see British-built cars stripped of their EEC status, stranding UK assembly plants on the wrong side of European customs barriers.
But look at the assembly lines in Sunderland or the engine plants across the Midlands, and the question of which way is Britain better off gets really serious. Tens of thousands of highly skilled, high-wage jobs depend on delivery trucks rolling off cross-Channel ferries every hour. Nissan wasn't exaggerating when it warned ministers that failing to adjust tariffs risks turning the country into a transit corridor. If British-assembled cars are shut out of European procurement schemes, the export volume that keeps the factories open will disappear overnight. A nation cannot build a strong future by buying cheap imported cars if its workers lose jobs that pay to buy them in the first place.
Then there is the diplomatic hostage trapped right in the crosshairs: Jaguar Land Rover. While volume producers like Nissan and Mini focus on European buyers, JLR has spent over a decade feeding on the appetite of the Chinese luxury market. But competition from homegrown Chinese electric off-roaders and shifting consumer loyalties saw JLR's sales in China drop from 146,000 units in 2017 down to 62,400 vehicles in the last financial year. If Britain puts up massive tariffs on Chinese models, Beijing will strike back with retaliatory levies targeting the new Range Rover Sport. Government insiders have concluded that while denting JLR's Chinese balance sheet is a painful blow, cutting off the British automotive industry from Europe would be a fatal mistake.
Once you strip away the political grandstanding, where does the national interest lie? If your idea of being better off begins and ends with letting a private individual lease a brand-new electric crossover for $343 a month, then keeping the borders open and laughing off European tariffs feels like a victory. It supercharges the transition away from fossil fuels, breaks the pricing power of legacy manufacturers, and puts fresh tech on every driveway. But a country cannot survive as a consumer of foreign state subsidies while dismantling the industrial muscle that pays its tax base. Cheap cars are a hollow triumph if they are bought on the ashes of our domestic manufacturing sector, leaving our skilled workforce with nothing to build and nowhere to export.
Britain's long-term prosperity seems to be tied to keeping the European Union on its side. Falling into line with Brussels is a bitter blow to trade autonomy, and it will inflict short-term pain on car buyers. But tariff independence is worthless if it isolates your country from the $94 single market that keeps your production lines on. Choosing cheap Chinese imports without tariffs would buy consumer euphoria for a brief moment, only to leave our automotive towns devastated and our assembly plants gone. Swallowing the tariff pill and standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Europe is the harder, more expensive route, but it is the only road that keeps Britain's industrial engine running. And the next logical step is to convince the Chinese automakers to start making EVs in the UK.
