high_priority_articles.title: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese EVs as EU trade rules loom - FleetPoint
high_priority_articles.summary: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese EVs as EU trade rules loom  FleetPoint
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Britain is considering tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the rapid growth of Chinese-owned brands intensifies pressure on the UK automotive industry.
According to reports, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is drawing up options for additional duties on Chinese vehicle imports. The move follows concerns that heavily subsidised Chinese manufacturers could be “dumping” vehicles into the UK market.
No tariffs have yet been announced. A UK government spokesperson told
: “We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”
The timing is significant for fleet operators. Chinese-owned brands are gaining market share rapidly, while the European Union is developing new measures designed to strengthen domestic automotive manufacturing and reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains.
Chinese cars surge in UK market
The strength of Chinese manufacturers in Britain was underlined by September’s new car registrations.
The SMMT reported 350,518 new cars registered during September, up 12.1% year on year. Battery electric registrations reached a record 99,199, up 36.3%, while plug-in hybrid registrations rose 55.7% to 59,563.
Chinese-owned brands accounted for 27.5% of the September market, according to analysis of the SMMT figures. That means more than one in four new cars registered during the crucial September plate-change month came from a Chinese-owned manufacturer. The year-to-date share has exceeded 21%.
BYD alone registered 20,140 cars in September, giving it a 5.75% market share. Chery recorded 9,788 registrations, while Chinese-owned brands including MG and Jaecoo also performed strongly.
The Jaecoo 7 was particularly notable. It became Britain’s best-selling new car in September, with more than 15,000 registrations according to SMMT data reported by the automotive press.
For fleet managers, the significance goes beyond brand recognition. Chinese manufacturers are increasingly competing through competitive pricing, extensive equipment levels and rapidly expanding dealer networks. They are also helping push down the cost of electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles.
Is Britain following the EU?
The answer is partly, but the situation is more complicated than simply copying Brussels.
The European Commission proposed its Industrial Accelerator Act in March. The legislation would introduce “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements for public procurement and public support in strategic sectors, including cars and batteries. It is designed to strengthen European manufacturing and reduce strategic dependencies on non-EU suppliers.
The proposal is not, however, a blanket ban on Chinese vehicles or a general import tariff.
The concern for Britain comes from the potential consequences for UK manufacturers and supply chains. The EU is considering rules that could favour European production when public money is involved. UK-built vehicles, batteries and components could potentially receive less favourable treatment unless Britain secures an appropriate relationship with the new framework.
The SMMT has warned that excluding Britain would damage an automotive sector that remains deeply integrated with Europe. Its analysis says UK automotive production directly supports €24 billion of economic activity in the EU and 250,000 jobs.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said: “Excluding the UK from ‘Made in Europe’ would be an own goal, weakening competitiveness, reducing scale and limiting consumer choice.”
The UK government is therefore seeking recognition as a “trusted partner” under the proposed EU arrangements.
There is another issue that matters even more immediately. From 1 January 2027, stricter rules of origin for electric vehicles under the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement are scheduled to apply. Vehicles that fail to meet the requirements could face a 10% tariff when traded between Britain and the EU.
This is separate from the Industrial Accelerator Act, but the two developments have become closely connected in the automotive sector.
Could Chinese EVs enter the EU through Britain?
This is one of Brussels’ concerns.
The EU has already imposed additional duties on Chinese battery electric vehicles following its investigation into Chinese government subsidies. The measures sit alongside the EU’s normal import duty and vary between manufacturers.
BYD faces a 17% countervailing duty, Geely 18.8% and SAIC 35.3%. Other cooperating manufacturers face 20.7%, while non-cooperating companies face 35.3%. The EU also applies its standard 10% import duty to these vehicles.
That means the effective EU tariff burden can reach about 45% for manufacturers subject to the highest additional duty.
Britain did not introduce equivalent measures. As a result, Chinese-built vehicles entering the UK face the standard UK tariff rather than an EU-style anti-subsidy duty.
That difference matters if the EU tightens its rules further. Brussels does not want Britain to become an easy route into the European market for vehicles that face substantially higher costs when entering the EU directly.
A Reuters report in September said the EU had urged Britain to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely with European trade policy. One EU official was quoted as saying: “A customs union would solve most of the problems of ‘made in Europe’.”
The UK government, however, has stressed that its trade policy will be determined independently.
Are Chinese manufacturers actually dumping cars?
This is perhaps the most important question.
“Dumping” has a specific meaning under trade law. It generally involves exporting goods at a price below their normal value, with evidence that this causes or threatens injury to domestic industry.
The EU has already concluded that Chinese BEV manufacturers benefit from government subsidies and that those subsidies threaten economic injury to European producers.
That does not automatically establish dumping in the UK.
In fact, the UK government confirmed in July that the independent Trade Remedies Authority had not initiated an investigation into Chinese electric vehicles. Ministers said Britain remained concerned about “overcapacity and underlying market distorting practices” but stressed that any action would have to serve UK industry.
That distinction is important. The rapid increase in Chinese vehicle registrations is clear evidence of competitive pressure, but high sales alone do not prove unlawful dumping.
Chinese manufacturers may also be winning customers because they offer competitive products at attractive prices. The September figures show that British buyers and fleet operators are responding strongly to that proposition.
What level could UK tariffs reach?
There is no confirmed UK tariff rate at present.
The most frequently discussed benchmark is the EU’s maximum effective rate of around 45%, combining the normal 10% import duty with the highest countervailing duty.
Reports suggest Britain could consider matching the EU approach. That does not necessarily mean every Chinese EV would attract a 45% tariff. A UK system could follow the EU model, with different rates according to manufacturer and the findings of a trade-remedies investigation.
The UK could therefore impose additional duties in the region of the EU’s 17% to 35.3% countervailing rates, on top of the existing 10% tariff. But any final figure would need to follow the UK’s own legal and economic assessment.
The government has already demonstrated that it is willing to use this mechanism. In August, the Trade Remedies Authority recommended provisional anti-dumping measures on Chinese boom lifts after finding that dumped imports had caused or were causing injury to UK industry.
That precedent suggests the UK has the machinery to act, but an automotive investigation would still require evidence.
What does this mean for fleets?
For fleet operators, tariffs could create both risks and opportunities.
Higher duties would probably increase the cost of affected Chinese-built vehicles, although manufacturers could absorb some of the increase to protect market share. Leasing companies and fleet buyers would also need to reassess whole-life costs, residual values and monthly rental rates.
There is also a wider question around competition.
Chinese manufacturers have helped accelerate the UK’s transition towards electrification by bringing more affordable EVs and PHEVs to the market. September’s figures demonstrate just how quickly customers are embracing that choice.
The government therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It wants to protect British automotive manufacturing and maintain access to the EU market without undermining competition or making electric vehicles less affordable.
For now, the key point is that Britain has not introduced tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is considering its options at a time when Chinese-owned brands are taking an increasingly large share of the UK market.
The eventual decision is likely to be shaped by three competing priorities: protecting UK automotive manufacturing, maintaining frictionless trade with Europe and keeping electric vehicles affordable for consumers and fleets.
The outcome could have a significant influence on Britain’s fleet market as the country moves towards its increasingly demanding zero-emission vehicle targets.

high_priority_articles.title: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means - Al Jazeera
high_priority_articles.summary: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means  Al JazeeraSaudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey trigger mutual defence pact  Financial TimesPakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey Trigger Mutual Defense Pact Over Houthi Attacks  Foreign PolicyPakistan Says Mecca Pact Is Supporting Saudi Arabia With Houthis  Bloomberg.comTurkey and Pakistan pledge to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia  Le Monde.fr
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Islamabad, Pakistan — For the first time since it was signed in August, the Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is now in force.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the pact’s top committee agreed to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, which is backing an offensive against Yemen’s Houthis.
“The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties,” said a joint statement shared by Pakistan’s Foreign Office.
The statement did not specify the size or role of the forces.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were supporting a counteroffensive by the internationally recognised Yemeni government to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.
Hours after the meeting, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part.
“The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role. We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces, and they are the ones retaking those areas,” Asif told Geo News, speaking from Riyadh on Monday night.
That leaves Pakistan in a defensive role alongside a Saudi offensive. Analysts told Al Jazeera that it raises a question Islamabad has yet to answer publicly: How long can it stay out of the actual fighting?
What is already in place?
Pakistan already had a military presence in Saudi Arabia. It has trained Saudi military personnel since 1967, with a 1982 agreement formalising the deputation of troops to the kingdom.
A declassified CIA assessment from June 1985 estimated that 13,000 to 14,000 Pakistanis were serving in the Saudi army, including an armoured brigade at Tabuk. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan also sent a large contingent to the kingdom for defensive duties.
Pakistan also signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia in September 2025, which treats aggression against either country as aggression against both.
In April, Riyadh confirmed that a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the Eastern Province.
Pakistan has not disclosed how many of its troops are in Saudi Arabia.
In September, Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), told the Saudi outlet Arab News that Pakistani forces were already deployed to protect the kingdom and its holy sites.
“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”
ISPR did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the deployment agreed upon in Riyadh.
On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said in a post on X that the country’s commitment to the security of the holy sites and the kingdom was not negotiable.
“The operational details of the actualisation of the collective deterrence are a matter of operational confidentiality and may not be made subject of media speculation,” the ministry said.
Turkiye’s footprint is less clear.
Asif said Turkish forces were also present, but Ankara has not publicly confirmed any deployment.
“There is no publicly acknowledged standing Turkish deployment in Saudi Arabia,” Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera.
Ereli noted that under Article 92 of Turkiye’s constitution, the authority to send troops abroad rests with the parliament, which has yet to ratify the Mecca pact.
What could deterrence look like?
Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, said Riyadh wants the pact to carry real weight.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to turn the Mecca pact from a political declaration into a deterrent,” she told Al Jazeera.
For now, she said, Riyadh mainly wants Pakistan and Turkiye to help defend Saudi territory and reinforce its air and missile defences, showing that another attack is no longer only a Saudi-Houthi matter. The Houthis have attacked multiple Saudi cities and facilities, including the East-West Pipeline that Riyadh has been using to export oil amid Iranian restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz during the ongoing war waged by the US.
Saudi authorities said two airports in the kingdom had been hit on Monday evening, injuring at least three people.
But Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman’s account of the meeting went further than what Thafer suggested.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” he wrote on X.
Thafer said the wording was deliberate.
“‘All those responsible’ is intentionally ambiguous. It tells the Houthis that Saudi Arabia may go beyond intercepting missiles and strike any actor or infrastructure enabling those attacks. It is also simultaneously warning external sponsors that Riyadh is watching the entire support network,” she said.
However, Pakistani officials have been more cautious.
“The document itself says, first, that it is defensive in nature. It has no offensive agenda,” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said at a news conference in Islamabad on October 2.
Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, said Pakistan’s contribution was likely to be specialised rather than large.
“Pakistan is most likely going to beef up its existing presence with air defence units, drones, battlefield communication systems and offensive cyber specialists, men from the corps of engineers to lay and lift mines, some special service troops. Nothing more than that, I would say,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ereli expects Turkiye’s role to be similarly limited.
“The realistic response would be calibrated and mostly non-ground. That means diplomatic coordination, intelligence sharing, emergency resupply of air defence, drones and electronic warfare, and perhaps naval or air-defence assets,” he said.
Could it extend into Yemen?
Thafer said two campaigns were now running side by side.
“There are really two concentric operations taking place: one is defending Saudi Arabia; the second is changing the military balance inside Yemen so the Houthis cannot continue attacking Saudi territory from a position of growing strength,” she said.
Pakistan has not said publicly where its role stops.
Asked by reporters in Rome on September 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, Asif did not answer directly.
“I’m not going into detail, but obviously, when I say that we are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia, that means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.
Pakistan has faced this question before.
In April 2015, its parliament unanimously resolved that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”. But the resolution also pledged that Pakistan would stand with Saudi Arabia if its territorial integrity were violated or the holy sites threatened.
Monday’s joint statement justified the deployment in similar terms and condemned the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina.
Tehran, though, is watching closely. On Sunday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for war in Yemen were untrue. He warned that any new intervention would only complicate the situation.
At the same news conference last week, Dar said he had raised the pact with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York in September, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.
“I made them aware that we are in a defence pact, and as Muslims, we have to honour it, and God willing, we will,” he said.
He said the Iranian leaders had suggested engaging the Houthis politically rather than through military action. Monday’s statement made no mention of a political track.
Javad Heiran-Nia, an analyst with the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran draws a clear distinction between defending Saudi territory and infrastructure and attacking the Houthis in Yemen.
“In general, if Pakistan’s deployment is purely defensive and limited to the protection of Saudi installations, Tehran can tolerate it. However, if Pakistan joins offensive operations against the Houthis, Iran regards it as a red line, since it views the Houthis as part of its strategic depth in the Arabian Peninsula,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Currently, Pakistan’s mediation has shifted from neutrality to management of conflicting interests, and its credibility is highly fragile,” he added.
Institute of Policy Studies’ Yamin, too, said the onus was on Islamabad.
“Pakistan needs to draw its red lines carefully to prevent its troops [from] getting involved in combat operations against the Houthis. So the question should [be] not how will they get involved but how can they prevent getting involved,” he said.

Much depends on what Riyadh wants from Yemen.

high_priority_articles.summary: US spice industry seeks tariff shield for India  IANS LIVE
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Washington, Oct 7 (IANS) The US spice industry is seeking continued tariff exemptions for Indian spices and wants the protection made permanent as Washington and New Delhi move towards a trade agreement, arguing that many of the products cannot be grown commercially in the United States.
Donald Pratt, president of the American Spice Trade Association (ASTA), said the industry's priority was to preserve tariff exemptions for agricultural products unavailable domestically but widely used by American consumers and businesses.
“Well, for our industry, it's about the continued exemption, you know, from tariffs, of agriculture that's not grown in this hemisphere and cannot be grown in this hemisphere, but that is beloved by our consumers, you know, and our business partners, worldwide,” Pratt told IANS at an event at India House in Washington.
Pratt said the Indian Embassy and others involved in the negotiations had already undertaken significant advocacy on the issue.
“But also I think as they go to wrap up the next phase of that, we hope that that continues the exemption now that we're seeing and becomes hopefully permanently, you know, enshrined, you know, as an exception to tariffs,” he said.
Pratt's comments put a spotlight on a segment of India-US commerce in which the American industry argues imports are essential because domestic production cannot meet demand.
Addressing the gathering separately, Pratt said India grows more than half of the 109 spices recognised by the International Organization for Standardization and is an essential supplier to the US industry.
The United States is the largest market for Indian spices, importing about $700 million worth last year, according to figures cited by Pratt.
“Here's the reality for our industry. The United States grows only a small fraction of the spices we use. Many spices simply can't be grown here at scale,” he said.
Pratt said the industry had spent considerable effort explaining why spices should be treated differently when tariffs were being considered.
He said there was now greater recognition that many spices are tied to particular climates and growing conditions and cannot simply be replaced with US production.
“So we rely on India for cumin, fennel, chilies, and dozens more spices,” he said. “They season the food Americans enjoy every day.”
Pratt said ASTA had worked closely with the Indian Embassy on tariffs over the past 18 months and described those discussions as “open, practical, collaborative”.
The association also mounted its own campaign to keep spices outside new tariff barriers.
“Asta led the industry advocacy for spices to be exempt from new, tariffs,” Pratt said.
“Our advocacy paid off last year with most spices included on exemption lists for Section 122 as well as 301 tariffs as unavailable natural resources,” he said.
“And as India and the US move towards a final trade agreement, we're hopeful for further considerations that keep spices accessible and affordable.”
The industry's case is built partly around the argument that tariffs on spices unavailable in the United States would raise costs without providing protection to a significant competing domestic industry.
Roberto Fanni, who chairs ASTA's science and regulatory committee, said the association had secured exemptions for spices because the United States was not a major producer.
“However, spices are exempt because it's recognized that US is not a producer of spices, so there is no any national production that can be, I would say pushed if there is a ban or there are tariffs for spices,” he told IANS.
Fanni said the relationship between suppliers in India and the US market was also evolving, with Indian producers increasingly understanding American requirements.
“The spice trace is definitely strategic. It's growing and it's really amazing to see how the relationship between the two countries are getting better,” he said.
He said suppliers and producers in India were addressing food safety and compliance issues from the farm level to make products more readily acceptable in the United States and allow trade volumes to expand.
Laura Schumer, executive director of the American Spice Trade Association, said India occupies a central position in the industry's supply chain.
“India is absolutely our most critical trade partner,” Schumer told IANS.
“Historically, we've relied so heavily on India, both for the breadth of spices, the volume of spices, and the value of spices that we import into the United States. India is our most critical trade partner, bar none.”
Schumer said the association represents about 100 companies that import, process, manufacture and sell spices in the United States. The India House event brought industry members together with government representatives and organisations working across the food and agriculture supply chain.
India and the United States have a broad trade relationship spanning goods and services, with tariffs and market access among the issues that have periodically produced differences between the two sides. Agriculture is particularly sensitive because trade policy can directly affect domestic producers, importers and consumers.
The spice industry's position distinguishes products that can be produced domestically from those that cannot be grown commercially in the United States. ASTA's case is that exempting unavailable natural resources such as many spices allows American businesses to maintain supplies without undermining comparable US agricultural production.

For listeners new to the topic, we encourage you to listen to the original episode first for essential background and context.
October 2026
The critical minerals landscape has continued to evolve largely in line with the trends identified here in this podcast episode. China has maintained its strategic focus on rare earths and other critical minerals, but the emphasis has increasingly shifted from simply controlling exports to strengthening oversight, traceability and licensing across the entire rare earth value chain. Recent measures have further centralised state oversight of rare earth production and processing, while export licensing requirements for key heavy rare earth elements remain in force.
At the same time, the temporary suspension of certain broader export-control measures has broadly remained in place, providing some short-term relief to manufacturers, although the underlying licensing framework continues to create uncertainty for companies dependent on Chinese supply.
Outside of China, governments and industry bodies have accelerated efforts to diversify supply chains, reflecting our conclusion that long-term dependence on Chinese processing capacity remains a strategic risk. The U.S., EU and partner countries have continued to invest in alternative mining, refining and magnet-production capabilities, while automotive, defence and technology companies have sought to secure alternative rare earth supplies and increase stockpiling where possible.
However, recent market disruption and reports of supply shortages in sectors such as automotive manufacturing underline the continued reality that China’s dominance is greatest in processing and refining rather than extraction, meaning that meaningful diversification is still likely to take many years. As a result, businesses are increasingly focusing on supply-chain mapping, contingency planning and regulatory compliance alongside efforts to develop alternative sourcing options.
January 2026
Joined by Stephanie Sun, International Trade Partner in Shanghai, Emerson and Stephanie unpack why these minerals are vital for modern industry and how their applications span clean energy, electronics, medical devices, and military technologies.
Emerson and Stephanie break down which minerals are considered “critical” in the US, EU, and China, highlighting the common goal of securing materials for advanced manufacturing and energy security. Good morning. Today, our trade correspondent explains why Germany’s volte-face on standing up to Chinese trade threats is too little, too late for many other EU capitals. And Moldova’s premier tells me that the country is already primed to start closing EU accession chapters — if Brussels keeps up its end of the bargain.
Converted
Four years after Germany’s Zeitenwende on foreign and defence policy, Berlin has made another “turning point” on trade, with a call to raise barriers against China. Many of its EU allies think it’s not a moment too soon, writes Andy Bounds.
Context: Germany’s manufacturers were until recently as reliant on China’s consumers as they were on cheap Russian gas. Germany has long opposed tougher action against Beijing, even as its trade deficit has ballooned.
But yesterday Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanded strong action to save Europe from Chinese exports. In a letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen with French President Emmanuel Macron, Merz called for tougher trade measures and a new instrument to quickly close the EU market to countries that do not play by the rules.
No country was mentioned but with trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič off to Beijing on Thursday the target was clear. Šefčovič has called the EU’s roughly €1bn a day trade deficit with China “unsustainable” and a threat to the European social model.
The two leaders say that “a massive industrial shock is affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance”, referring to pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools and chemicals industries.
It comes just two years after Germany declined to back the imposition of anti-subsidy duties on Chinese electric vehicles — a fact remarked upon by member states who have been calling for tougher action against Beijing for years.
“Germany is pragmatic,” said one EU diplomat. “As long as China was buying its cars and machinery it didn’t want to pick a fight. Now it is damaging the economy, that has changed.”
“Germany has long been the most reluctant EU member state, but Berlin finally seems to have seen the light,” said a second.
Officially Berlin still tries to comply with WTO rules and refrains from naming China as the main culprit. The problem, German officials say, is “unfair practices” and “distorted competition”.
A German official acknowledged that the combination of falling German exports to China and surging Chinese imports had triggered a shift.
“Industry has moved and political parties especially, the [ruling centre-right] CDU as well,” they said.
Chart du jour: Bonds and barricades
France is being hit by a pre-election debt sell-off that could spill into a full-blown financial crisis. Many fear it could shake the entire Eurozone.
Closing time
Moldova is already technically able to close at least seven of its 33 EU accession stages, its prime minister has said, as he urged Brussels to provide a “window” for securing membership in the next two years.
Context: Moldova is one of four candidates — alongside Ukraine, Montenegro and Albania — assessed by Brussels as frontrunners for membership. The former Soviet republic has been constantly targeted by Russian propaganda urging citizens to oppose western integration. Its pro-EU president Maia Sandu steps down in October 2028.
“Let’s be pragmatic here. We don’t have time to lose. We need to use this window,” Vasile Tofan told the FT. “We need not lose the big picture. We need to get this country into Europe.”
Tofan said that Moldova had already enacted reforms that would allow it “to close seven to 10” of the European Commission’s accession milestones, known as “chapters”.
His government has devised a consultancy-style Gantt chart detailing how it can complete all the chapters in early 2028.
Tofan also said he expected the Commission to give it a glowing assessment in a progress report this month: “Everything I’ve heard, also between the lines, is that we’re going to get a good report at the end of October. We’re going to continue to be a good pupil in this classroom and we’ll continue advancing on this path.”
He waved away talk of enlargement reforms and internal EU politics that could stymie Chisinau’s progress as “above our pay grade . . . We’re just focusing on things we can control, and we believe it should be merit-based.”
Tofan said Moldova had secured Romanian gas supplies for next winter and is “pursuing long-term energy partnerships with friendly and reliable partners such as Azerbaijan”. The country’s exports to the EU have risen 11 per cent so far this year, exceeding the bloc’s economic growth.
“We bet everything on [EU membership]. So in terms of population feedback, if we don’t advance, I think the chance of Russian sentiment spiking in Moldova is very high,” he added.

Gold has played a key role in human’s history as it has been widely used as a store of value and medium of exchange. Currently, apart from its shine and usage for jewelry, the precious metal is widely seen as a safe-haven asset, meaning that it is considered a good investment during turbulent times. Gold is also widely seen as a hedge against inflation and against depreciating currencies as it doesn’t rely on any specific issuer or government.
Central banks are the biggest Gold holders. In their aim to support their currencies in turbulent times, central banks tend to diversify their reserves and buy Gold to improve the perceived strength of the economy and the currency. High Gold reserves can be a source of trust for a country’s solvency. Central banks added 1,136 tonnes of Gold worth around $70 billion to their reserves in 2022, according to data from the World Gold Council. This is the highest yearly purchase since records began. Central banks from emerging economies such as China, India and Turkey are quickly increasing their Gold reserves.
Gold has an inverse correlation with the US Dollar and US Treasuries, which are both major reserve and safe-haven assets. When the Dollar depreciates, Gold tends to rise, enabling investors and central banks to diversify their assets in turbulent times. Gold is also inversely correlated with risk assets. A rally in the stock market tends to weaken Gold price, while sell-offs in riskier markets tend to favor the precious metal.
The price can move due to a wide range of factors. Geopolitical instability or fears of a deep recession can quickly make Gold price escalate due to its safe-haven status. As a yield-less asset, Gold tends to rise with lower interest rates, while higher cost of money usually weighs down on the yellow metal. The Polymarket contract on 2026 Fed cuts measures how many reductions the central bank delivers during the calendar year. At the October 6 data retrieval, the event showed $53.9M in total volume and $4.18M in liquidity; those figures describe activity in the contract, not the depth of Bitcoin liquidity or a forecast of crypto flows.

The Fed raised its target range by 25 basis points in September, to 3.75%-4.00%, after a December 2025 cut had lowered it to 3.50%-3.75%. The September dot plot put the median federal funds rate at 4.1% by year-end, while most participants anticipated at least one further increase.
The primary market description points to solid economic expansion, unemployment around 4.1%-4.2%, and core inflation near 3.4% as reasons a restrictive stance remains plausible. Softer inflation readings have complicated the timing. Reuters reported that August personal consumption expenditures inflation rose 3.4% year over year, below the 3.7% estimate in its economist poll.
After that data, Goldman Sachs and several other brokerages shifted their expected next 25-basis-point hike from October toward December. The PCE reading also matters to risk assets because inflation that eases without prompting cuts can still leave real rates restrictive.
What the 96% Price Proves and What It Does Not
The zero-cut price had slipped 0.1 percentage points over 24 hours. The event remained open and was scheduled to close on January 1, 2027, so these readings reflect traders’ risk-taking rather than a settled outcome or a poll of market participants.
Crucially, a zero-cut contract is not a hike contract. It counts reductions, so the Fed could hold rates through year-end, and the outcome could still resolve as zero cuts; a further increase would also leave the number of cuts at zero. That distinction explains how Polymarket’s no-cut pricing can coexist with brokerage forecasts that mostly call for one more quarter-point hike.
The market’s strongest conclusion is that traders see little room for easing in 2026, not that they agree on the terminal rate or the next meeting’s decision. For crypto, that keeps the policy backdrop restrictive: higher rates can weigh on risk appetite and financing conditions, but the contract alone does not establish a direction or magnitude for Bitcoin’s next move.
Late-October and December Decisions Remain the Big Tests
The October and December meetings, along with the upcoming inflation and labor market reports, are the next key tests identified in the market description. Reuters reported that CME FedWatch had put the odds of an October hike near 38%, down from almost 71% a week earlier, illustrating how quickly expectations can shift as data arrives.
A hold in October would leave December as the central decision point for brokerages forecasting another increase. An October hike would reinforce the restrictive path, while cooler inflation and weaker labor readings could reduce the case for a second move without reopening the case for a cut.
The market assigns near-total weight to no cuts, yet the path to that outcome remains sensitive to data and meeting-by-meeting decisions. Traders tracking the Federal Reserve should treat the Polymarket price as a probability for one defined calendar-year outcome, not as a precise timetable for policy or a direct signal of Bitcoin liquidity.

The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Private equity dealmakers might have thought the worst of the rising interest rate environment of a few years ago was behind them. But after a fall since late 2024, rates are moving back up.
Last month, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates a quarter point to 4 percent. The move, the first increase since July 2023, was in response to inflation and the surge in oil prices spurred on by the conflicts in the Middle East.
What will this new upward cycle mean for private equity? Will it have an appreciable effect on dealmaking? And if so, in what ways?
PE Hub posed these questions to a diverse array of professionals and leaders in the private equity community. Though nearly all agreed the interest rate hike could affect the exit climate, there was no consensus on how or to what extent the increase would be felt in dealmaking.
Jason Cohen, managing director and head of investment banking, Portage Point Partners
“Yes, an increase in interest rates will likely have a further financial impact on private equity dealmaking, but this is not totally new territory for them. Private equity has already been dealing with higher-for-longer interest rates in their dealmaking for the last several years. This increased cost of debt has generally limited leverage levels and negatively affects the returns available to private equity investors.
“As a result, private equity investors have spent more time conducting diligence on deals, which in turn has elongated sale processes. Even once private equity pulls the trigger and closes on a deal, their focus must remain on operational improvements and ‘working the asset’ to ensure value creation and strong returns at exit. If the rate raise is viewed as a sign of more to come, it could further impact dealmaking for deals where the math already was tight.”
Howard Gutman, director of private equity services, Highspring
“For PE firms with capital deploying in the next few months, a quarter point makes the cost of acquiring an asset marginally more expensive than it was. That’s real, but it’s marginal. The harder problem has been the exit environment, and that predates this decision.
“Sponsors have spent the last year hunting for the right windows and the right slivers to exit into. A single hike doesn’t close those windows. It just reinforces that the assets, which are structurally attractive, will still clear, and the ones that aren’t, will keep waiting. Deal timing tightens. It doesn’t stop.”
Mark Radzik, co-founder and managing partner, Granite Creek Capital Partners
“Conventional wisdom is that a tightening cycle will slow transaction volumes. We believe the lower middle market will be less affected, because our returns are driven primarily by operational improvements and by growing companies to the scale where they command higher multiples at exit.”
Kevin Tom, founder and managing partner, Skyline Investors
“I’d say the rate environment doesn’t affect Skyline’s dealmaking given we don’t utilize a lot of third-party debt to finance our transactions. Our fund has the unique capability to invest up and down the capital structure and can bring in third-party debt when we choose to.”
Kevin Mulligan, managing director, investment team, Monomoy Capital Partners
“Across the industry, higher rates make it harder to rely on leverage to support returns: the math simply isn’t as forgiving as it used to be. Great businesses will still trade, but the marginal decisions become that much tougher. That’s why operational value creation, growing EBITDA and improving the underlying business matters more than ever. You can’t count on multiple expansion or cheap debt to do the work.”
Justin Abelow, managing director, Houlihan Lokey’s Financial Sponsors Group
“While rate raises are clearly a net negative for PE dealmaking, their impact should prove more muted as you move deeper into the middle market: the value creation playbook for smaller companies has long been more dependent on operating improvements than on leverage magic. It’s easier, after all, to maneuver the proverbial nimble destroyer than a lumbering battleship.”

CHIPS Act incentives, reshoring, and investment in advanced packaging help capture AI, 5G, and automotive demand while reducing supply chain risk
Dublin, Oct. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- "US Advanced Semiconductor Packaging Market - Strategic Insights and Forecasts (2026-2031)" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering.
The US advanced semiconductor packaging market is projected to increase from USD 9.6 billion in 2026 to USD 11.7 billion by 2031, registering a CAGR of 4.1%. Market growth is supported by rising demand for compact, high-performance semiconductor modules across artificial intelligence, 5G telecommunications, autonomous systems, automotive electronics, data centers, defense, and aerospace applications.
Advanced packaging technologies are becoming increasingly important for high-density interconnects, thermal management, electrical performance, and heterogeneous integration. Federal support through the CHIPS and Science Act is encouraging domestic semiconductor manufacturing and packaging investment. NIST-led research into polymer materials is also addressing mechanical stress in multi-die stacks, strengthening efforts to expand US production capacity and reduce dependence on overseas supply chains.
Key Market Drivers
Federal subsidies under the CHIPS Act are reducing capital barriers for domestic semiconductor operations and accelerating investment in flip-chip, fan-out, and embedded-die packaging. Growth in AI infrastructure is another major driver as data centers adopt high-bandwidth memory, high-performance computing systems, and heterogeneous integration technologies.
Demand for 2.5D and 3D stacking is increasing because these technologies help semiconductor manufacturers address power density, signal integrity, and system performance requirements. Adoption is expanding across commercial, automotive, telecommunications, and defense applications. Domestic hyperscalers are also prioritizing local sourcing to improve supply chain resilience and support access to advanced semiconductor packaging services.
Market Challenges
Geopolitical disruption, tariffs, and import restrictions affecting essential polymer materials can increase production costs and delay shipments. Mechanical stress within multi-die stacks may contribute to yield losses and limit confidence in high-volume manufacturing commitments.
The market also faces limited domestic expertise and capacity in soft materials, including underfills and dielectrics. Continued reliance on Asian suppliers exposes US semiconductor companies to tariffs, logistics constraints, and material shortages. These challenges are particularly significant for automotive, aerospace, defense, and other high-reliability applications requiring strict quality and performance standards.
Packaging Type Insights
- Flip-Chip: Leads market demand due to strong electrical and thermal performance. It supports high-density integration and reduced signal latency in AI, telecommunications, and automotive systems.
- Fan-Out Wafer-Level Packaging (FOWLP): Supports thin, high-performance semiconductor modules used in mobile devices and edge AI applications.
- Embedded Die: Enables compact integration of logic and memory for space-constrained and power-sensitive products.
- Others: Includes hybrid and emerging semiconductor packaging technologies designed for specialized performance requirements.
Application Insights
- Consumer Electronics: Generates substantial volume demand for high-density packages used in smartphones, wearable devices, and connected products.
- Automotive: Supports electric vehicles and advanced driver-assistance systems requiring thermal reliability and durable semiconductor components.
- Telecommunication: Enables 5G base stations, networking equipment, and optical communications through high-speed interconnects.
- Others: Includes industrial, defense, and aerospace applications.
End-User Insights
- Foundries: Use outsourced back-end packaging services to scale production efficiently while meeting domestic sourcing requirements associated with CHIPS-funded programs.
- Integrated Device Manufacturers (IDMs): Maintain advanced packaging capabilities to support proprietary AI, automotive, telecommunications, and high-performance computing products.
Competitive and Strategic Outlook
The US advanced semiconductor packaging market includes integrated semiconductor manufacturers and specialized outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers competing through production capacity, packaging technology, manufacturing efficiency, and yield optimization.
Intel is strengthening its position in embedded packaging for AI systems, supported by its Fab 9 facility in New Mexico. Amkor Technology is expanding its fan-out packaging and testing capabilities through a planned USD 7 billion campus in Arizona, including capacity intended to support automotive demand and TSMC-partnered production volumes.
Investment in domestic facilities, high-performance packaging equipment, materials research, and workforce expertise will remain central to competitive differentiation. Heterogeneous integration, 2.5D and 3D stacking, AI infrastructure, 5G deployment, and reshoring initiatives are expected to create long-term opportunities despite material supply and manufacturing yield constraints.

FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt.
FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks join forces to deliver landmark power interconnector to supply the DRC's Copperbelt
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC's Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation
Published on
6 Oct 2026
Kinshasa, 6 October 2026 – The Strategic Investment Fund of the Democratic Republic of the Congo ("FIS-RDC"), Enterprise Power DRC SARL ("EnPower"), Trafigura and Gridworks Development Partners (together, "the Parties") have signed a Strategic Framework Agreement to jointly finance, build and operate a 200km high-voltage power line connecting Kalumbila, Zambia, with Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The Kalumbila–Kolwezi Interconnector Project ("KKIP") will strengthen the DRC's connection to the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), the regional body that links national grids and allows countries to trade power across borders. The project has reached the final stage of development, with all necessary concessions, licences and authorisations secured. It has an estimated construction cost of USD300 million.
KKIP will deliver benefits on both sides of the border: a new source of reliable, affordable power for the DRC's mining and industrial sectors, and new export capacity and transmission opportunities for Zambian power producers. The line will have a thermal capacity of 700MW, enabling up to 550MW of competitively priced electricity to be imported into the Copperbelt mining region of the DRC. The line design allows for a future capacity increase to over 1GW.
The Parties and financing
FIS-RDC, EnPower and Gridworks have confirmed their intention to invest equity in KKIP, with Gridworks as lead equity investor and majority shareholder. The Parties are in discussions with Zambian entities about taking a stake in the project. EnPower is the project developer, a licensed Congolese power trader and a SAPP member. Gridworks is a specialist transmission and distribution developer owned and funded by British International Investment, the UK Government’s development finance institution. Trafigura, a market leader in the global commodities industry, has agreed to arrange a significant share of the project's debt financing.
For FIS-RDC, the transaction supports the DRC Government's objective of investing in strategic infrastructure with wider economic benefits. It is the first investment announced by FIS-RDC since its creation in October 2025.
Benefits for the DRC
KKIP will help address the country's structural energy deficit of more than 1GW. It is expected to:
Supply electricity from across Southern Africa to power Congolese mining and industry, supporting social and economic development in local communities.
Enable the development of mining and refining projects currently on hold due to a lack of available, cost-effective baseload power.
Increase mining and refining output, generating greater fiscal contributions for the DRC.
Deliver broader benefits for the DRC by expanding access to reliable, affordable power for communities and businesses, supporting local enterprise and jobs, and contributing to economic diversification.
Benefits for Zambia
KKIP will create export opportunities for Zambian power producers, provide transmission capacity for licensed operators, and help spur the development of new generation. The participation of FIS-RDC, alongside Gridworks and Trafigura, will also strengthen cooperation between the DRC and Zambian governments and create a platform for long-term investment. Discussions are already underway with Zambian entities on potential co-investment.
Emile Osumba, CEO of FIS-RDC, said: "KKIP is the Fund's inaugural transaction, and it reflects precisely the mandate entrusted to us by the Government. By helping close the Copperbelt's power deficit, the project will unlock industrial growth, skilled jobs and fiscal revenue for the DRC. By backing a project led by a private Congolese developer, FIS-RDC is demonstrating that sovereign capital can act as a catalyst for private investment rather than a substitute for it. And by co-investing alongside credible and experienced partners such as Gridworks, we are building the track record that will allow the Fund to mobilise further capital for the country's strategic infrastructure."
Marc Orphanides, Managing Director of EnPower, added: “This agreement is an important milestone towards executing this strategic transmission infrastructure, which will add significant capacity to meet the ever-growing power demand of the DRC mining industry. We are grateful to the authorities, stakeholders and communities in the DRC and Zambia, as well as the International Finance Corporation, for their support to KKIP, which will be the first privately developed and financed cross-border transmission infrastructure on the African continent.”
Gonzalo De Olazaval, Global Head of Metals and Minerals at Trafigura, commented: “Trafigura is proud to support this landmark power project in the DRC, part of our broader power strategy in Africa. Reliable, competitively priced power is a critical enabler of economic growth across the continent, and Trafigura is well placed to bring together the investment, infrastructure and partnerships needed to make these projects a reality. KKIP has the potential to unlock industrial growth in the DRC and Zambia, while also supporting job creation and local communities in both countries.”
Chris Flavin, CEO of Gridworks, said: “Gridworks is proud to be the lead equity investor in KKIP. This is an important regional integration project. Zambia and the DRC both stand to benefit from closer interconnection, and this project will give the Copperbelt access to reliable, competitively priced power and lay the foundation for further cross-border transmission investment across Southern Africa. While the project is anchored by mining offtake, there is capacity on the line to serve the wider population too. Connecting regional power markets and supporting efficient energy trading is key to sustained economic growth in the region. We look forward to working alongside our partners to deliver this important infrastructure."

high_priority_articles.full_text:
China accused a Philippine military aircraft of illegally entering airspace over the disputed area in the South China Sea, while Manila said a Chinese fighter jet interfered with its routine patrol by repeatedly flying in close proximity.
BEIJING: Beijing warned Manila on Monday (Oct 5) against "provocative acts" in the disputed South China Sea, accusing a Philippine aircraft of an airspace violation over the weekend.
Beijing claims most of the sea, despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and confrontations have occurred regularly.
The Philippine armed forces said a Chinese fighter jet had interfered with a "routine military patrol" carried out by a Cessna 208 turboprop near the Scarborough Shoal on Saturday (Oct 3).
The Chinese military's Southern Theater Command said that the Philippine plane had "illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's Huangyan Dao" - Beijing's name for the disputed shoal.
Chinese "naval and air forces... tracked and monitored the Philippine aircraft, and issued warnings to expel it in accordance with laws and regulations", military spokesman Zhai Shichen said in a statement shared on social media platform WeChat on Monday.
Senior Captain Zhai said the Philippines' actions "seriously violate China's sovereignty" and warned Manila "to stop rights violations and provocative acts immediately".
In a statement issued on Sunday, the Philippine armed forces said that a Chinese J-16 fighter had "repeatedly approached and manoeuvred in close proximity to the Philippine aircraft, including manoeuvring ahead of and around it and positioning itself within the Philippine aircraft's wake".
The Philippine government said a second confrontation occurred on Sunday in the Spratly Islands, further south in the South China Sea.
The weekend incidents came about two weeks after the Philippines said a China Coast Guard ship rammed one of its fisheries department boats in another area of the Spratlys.
Beijing subsequently blamed the actions of the Philippine vessel, which it said "bears full responsibility for the incident".

high_priority_articles.title: $2.5bn NEOM Sky Stadium Shelved as 46,000-seat Saudi Arabia's World Cup Project Loses Momentum - Construction Review
high_priority_articles.summary: $2.5bn NEOM Sky Stadium Shelved as 46,000-seat Saudi Arabia's World Cup Project Loses Momentum  Construction Review
high_priority_articles.full_text:
NEOM Sky Stadium plans have been shelved indefinitely, removing one of Saudi Arabia’s most ambitious proposed World Cup venues. The $2.5 billion stadium formed part of The Line, NEOM’s futuristic 160-kilometre development. The proposed venue would have seated more than 46,000 spectators.
Its pitch was planned more than 350 meters above ground level. However, delays and downsizing across The Line have changed the stadium’s construction outlook. Two sources familiar with the project confirmed its indefinite suspension to Reuters.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction plans hit The Line setback
NEOM Sky Stadium was designed as a signature sports landmark within The Line. Saudi Arabia’s official World Cup plans identify the project as NEOM Stadium. The “Sky Stadium” description reflects its extraordinary elevated design.
The stadium would have featured a pitch positioned more than 350 meters above ground. Its roof would have formed part of the surrounding city structure. Furthermore, the design aimed to create an integrated sports venue within The Line.
The proposed capacity stood at 46,010 spectators. The venue would have hosted group-stage and knockout matches during the 2034 World Cup. Those stages included the round of 32, round of 16 and quarter-final.
Initially, Saudi Arabia expected the stadium to reach completion by 2032. The venue also formed part of the country’s original 15-stadium World Cup proposal.
However, the stadium depended heavily on The Line’s wider construction program. That development has subsequently faced major delays and significant scope reductions.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction stalls alongside wider giga-project changes
NEOM Sky Stadium construction now faces an uncertain future after The Line lost priority. Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan confirmed that shift earlier this year. He also said The Line was not essential before its original 2030 target.
Nevertheless, Al-Rumayyan previously denied that Saudi Arabia had cancelled projects. The latest stadium decision therefore represents a significant change surrounding the ambitious development.
MEED Projects now lists the proposed stadium as “on hold”. The platform estimates its construction cost at approximately $2.5 billion. It currently provides no completion date for the venue.
The shelving also follows broader changes affecting Saudi Arabia’s expensive giga-project program. FreeYork reported that The Line underwent reviews amid concerns surrounding costs and delivery. Those pressures have contributed to reductions across the wider development.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia continues developing other World Cup construction projects. The country plans 15 venues across five host cities for the 2034 tournament. The overall stadium program carries an estimated value of $22.7 billion.
Saudi Arabia’s changing stadium construction program extends beyond NEOM, with the $20.4 billion Jeddah Central development also featuring a major sports stadium.
The Jeddah project covers 5.7 square kilometres and includes residential, hospitality, cultural and marine facilities. Its planned stadium forms part of five major construction packages that attracted contractor bids.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction leaves World Cup venue strategy evolving
NEOM Sky Stadium construction would have delivered one of the most unconventional football venues ever proposed. Its elevated location would have distinguished it from conventional stadium developments worldwide.
The venue was also intended to continue operating after the tournament. Saudi Arabia planned to make it home to NEOM SC’s professional football teams. It would additionally support sports and active-lifestyle programs within the city.
However, the project now has no confirmed construction schedule. Saudi Arabia’s World Cup authority told Reuters that substantial tournament construction milestones were progressing. It did not specifically address the stadium’s suspension.
Other venues continue moving forward despite the NEOM setback. Aramco Stadium in Al Khobar remains under construction and is expected to reach completion soon.
Saudi Arabia will host the first 48-team World Cup staged entirely within one country. The tournament will therefore require extensive construction, refurbishment and supporting infrastructure.
The NEOM decision highlights the construction risks associated with projects dependent on wider masterplans. Changes to The Line have consequently affected the stadium’s own delivery prospects.
For now, the $2.5 billion NEOM Sky Stadium remains on hold. Its proposed elevated arena has moved from an ambitious World Cup concept to an uncertain construction project.

high_priority_articles.summary: Philippines grants 30-day visa-free entry to South Africa, Kenya, the US and 44 other African countries, but leaves out Nigeria, China and India  Business Insider Africa
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- The Philippines now allows citizens of 46 African countries to enter visa-free for up to 30 days to boost tourism and investment.
- Travellers must have a passport valid for at least six months and a return or onward ticket to qualify.
- China and India are excluded from the general 30-day visa-free policy; Chinese visitors have up to 14 days visa-free with different rules.
- Tourists can extend their stay by 29 days for a total of 59 days, while the visa-free entry list covers 157 countries overall, with some special cases.
The Philippines is allowing citizens of 46 African countries, including South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda and Tanzania, to enter visa-free for up to 30 days, alongside travellers from the US, UK, Canada and Japan, while Nigeria, China and India remain outside the standard arrangement.
Under Executive Order No. 408 and subsequent amendments, eligible travellers must hold passports valid for at least six months beyond their planned stay and have a return or onward ticket.
African countries covered by the policy include South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Morocco, Rwanda, Senegal, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Other eligible countries include Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Republic of Congo, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea and Eritrea.
Gabon, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles, Eswatini, Togo and Tunisia also qualify.
However, nationals of Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan do not qualify for the Philippines’ standard 30-day visa-free entry and generally require a visa before travelling.
China and India, two of Asia’s largest economies, are also outside the arrangement, although both benefit from separate visa-free rules with shorter stays.
By contrast, citizens of major economies including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Japan, Germany, France and South Korea qualify for the 30-day visa-free arrangement.
Philippines targets more foreign visitors
The visa policy comes as Manila seeks to strengthen tourism’s contribution to the economy and make the country more accessible to overseas visitors.
The Philippines recorded about 5.94 million international tourists in 2025, while inbound visitor spending reached an estimated 694 billion Philippine pesos. Tourism contributed 8.1% to the economy and supported about 7.7 million jobs during the year.
International arrivals have continued to rise in 2026, with the government also pushing for better airports, transport links and international connectivity.
Tourism Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay said the government wants to show that the Philippines is “open, accessible, and ready for greater tourism and investment.”
Longer stays are possible
Travellers admitted under the 30-day visa-free arrangement can apply for an initial 29-day extension through the Philippine Bureau of Immigration, taking their authorised stay to 59 days.
The broader visa-free list covers 157 countries, although separate rules apply to some nationalities. Brazilian and Israeli passport holders, for instance, can enter visa-free for up to 59 days under existing bilateral agreements.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The strategic pivot was highlighted at the Phoenix Global Development Forum for Enterprises in Dar es Salaam, where government officials, business leaders, and academics convened to map the next phase of Sino-Tanzanian economic cooperation. For CRJE, the forum marked a transition from historical aid-driven projects to modern, commercial infrastructure development aligned with Tanzania's long-term economic blueprint.
From TAZARA to Modern Infrastructure
The company's Tanzanian footprint dates back to 1969, when its parent group, China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG), dispatched 1,114 employees to participate in the construction of TAZARA. This monumental infrastructure project was designed to link landlocked Zambia's copper belt to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, bypassing routes controlled by apartheid-era regimes in southern Africa.
During the initial construction phase, the Chinese team undertook approximately 506,400 square meters of building works along the railway line. This extensive effort included the construction of 93 stations, locomotive and rolling stock repair plants, technical training schools, depots, hospitals, and accommodation facilities. The project not only transformed regional logistics but also established a deep cultural and technical exchange between the two nations.
After TAZARA became operational, CRCEG retained a specialized team to undertake ongoing maintenance work along the railway corridor. The company formally registered its Tanzanian branch in Dar es Salaam in 2000, coinciding with the country's launch of Vision 2025. In 2013, as its business portfolio expanded beyond rail, the entity was rebranded as CRJE (East Africa) Limited, reflecting its broader mandate in the regional construction market.
Aligning with Dira 2050
Tanzania's newly articulated National Development Vision 2050, popularly known as Dira 2050, demands massive upgrades in transport, energy, and urban infrastructure to achieve middle-to-high-income economic status. The Phoenix Global Development Forum, co-organized by Phoenix TV and the Chinese Enterprises Association in Tanzania (CEAT), provided a platform for CRJE to outline its aspirations for this next developmental chapter.
The forum was attended by high-profile figures, including Minister of State in the President's Office for Planning and Investment, Prof Kitila Mkumbo, and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative Shigeki Komatsubara. Their presence underscored the institutional importance placed on foreign direct investment and public-private partnerships in realizing the nation's mid-century goals.
For CRJE, the transition to Dira 2050 involves moving beyond traditional civil works to encompass complex, technology-driven infrastructure projects. This includes modern port expansions, smart city developments, and large-scale irrigation schemes designed to support Tanzania's rapidly growing population and agricultural export ambitions. The company views its historical presence as a unique competitive advantage, offering institutional memory and established government relations that newer market entrants lack.
The Evolution of Sino-Tanzanian Cooperation
The trajectory of CRJE mirrors the broader evolution of Sino-African economic relations. In the 1970s, projects like TAZARA were primarily state-led aid initiatives, funded by concessional loans and driven by geopolitical solidarity. Today, the partnership is characterized by commercial contracts, joint ventures, and a focus on mutual economic benefit.
A critical component of this modern partnership is technology transfer and local capacity building. Echoing the technical training schools established during the TAZARA era, CRJE now emphasizes the employment and upskilling of Tanzanian engineers and project managers. This approach not only reduces operational costs but also fosters local goodwill and ensures that the technical expertise required to maintain complex infrastructure remains within the country.
Challenges and Future Prospects
Despite its deep roots, CRJE operates in an increasingly competitive and scrutinized market. Tanzanian authorities are placing greater emphasis on debt sustainability, environmental compliance, and the use of local subcontractors. International financial institutions and domestic civil society organizations frequently demand greater transparency regarding the terms of infrastructure financing and the long-term economic viability of mega-projects.
Furthermore, the company must navigate the complexities of Tanzania's evolving regulatory environment, which seeks to maximize local content and ensure that foreign investments translate into tangible job creation and skills development. As Tanzania pushes toward its mid-century economic goals, CRJE's evolution from a railway builder to a comprehensive infrastructure partner reflects the maturing, complex nature of foreign direct investment in East Africa. The success of this transition will depend on the firm's ability to balance commercial imperatives with the developmental priorities of its host nation.
Industry observers note that the next decade will be critical for CRJE as it competes against both Western contractors and other Asian firms for lucrative government tenders. To maintain its market leadership, the firm is increasingly integrating green building practices and renewable energy components into its project proposals, aligning with global climate finance requirements. Ultimately, CRJE's continued relevance in Tanzania will be measured not just by the volume of concrete poured, but by its contribution to sustainable, inclusive economic growth under the Dira 2050 framework.
