high_priority_articles.summary: Brussels Sets the New Customs Codes Ahead of the EUDR Rollout  Wood Central
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Commission has firmed up its customs codes in the weeks leading up to the EUDR rollout, with timber shipped into the 27-nation bloc from 30 December requiring a due diligence statement upon entry. That is according to the Commission’s deforestation team, which released the updated TARIC document for the EU Deforestation Regulation late last month and is poised to start a new round of online training later today.
“If the obligations are not met, import or export is prohibited,” the Commission’s customs directorate states in the document’s first edition, with code C716 telling customs that the company declaring the goods holds a due diligence statement for them. A container of sawn timber therefore takes the same code as a shipment of coffee, and timber leaving the EU takes it as well as timber arriving.
It comes as Brussels hands every statement to the national authority of the EU country where the operator is based from 15 October, under Implementing Regulation 2026/1565, with exporters outside the bloc assigned to a member state through their registration. Once a statement’s reference number reaches the company that lodged it, no authority can reject the statement, and that number is the one quoted beside the code.
Meanwhile, global exporters that clear their own timber into the EU are considered upstream operators under the Commission’s roles guidance and need a valid EU EORI number and registration in the system before they can lodge a statement. The first European company to sell that timber on is an operator too, so the same shipment needs two statements before it reaches a buyer.
Elsewhere on the declaration, customs now has codes for re-imports, samples, goods placed on the market before the rules apply, and a downstream company exporting goods already covered by a statement. Used goods and packing have their own codes too, following the carve-outs Brussels wrote into the product list, which removed used timber, bamboo, and loaded pallets from the regulation last month.
Under last December’s amendment, an importer’s first buyer keeps the reference number on file for at least five years and never passes it on, ending the forwarding of numbers down the chain that Austria’s sawmillers had warned would run into the hundreds of thousands. Large downstream operators and traders still register in the system, whilst smaller firms downstream only keep their records and report any product they suspect does not comply.
“With this package, we are providing the clarity and predictability that businesses, Member States and our international partners need,” Jessika Roswall, the European Commissioner for Environment, said in July when she adopted the system rules alongside the product list. The Commission runs the first of three online sessions for upstream operators today, with three more for micro and small primary producers on their one-off simplified declaration.
As it stands, large and medium operators must comply from 30 December, joined by micro and small firms already covered by the old EU Timber Regulation. Only a statement lodged on the system’s production server counts for customs, whilst its acceptance server takes practice statements that have no legal value.

high_priority_articles.title: Sanctions Relief Returns Belarusian Potash to US Ports as Prices Fall - Crux Investor
high_priority_articles.summary: Sanctions Relief Returns Belarusian Potash to US Ports as Prices Fall  Crux Investor
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- A 30,000-tonne cargo of Belarusian muriate of potash (MOP) is scheduled to discharge at New Orleans on October 14, the first US-bound Belarusian potash in four years.
- The US Treasury delisted Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company on March 26, 2026, reopening a channel that averaged 635,000 tonnes a year into the US from 2017 to 2021.
- The World Bank MOP benchmark fell from $405.00 per tonne in May 2026 to $367.50 in September, within $2.50 of its $365 forecast for 2027.
- Belarus mined 6 million tonnes of potassium oxide in 2025 against 49 million worldwide, but President Alexander Lukashenko said on September 21 that those volumes are contracted.
- A World Bank MOP price above $400 per tonne on November 3, 2026, would indicate demand absorbed returning Belarusian supply rather than displaced Canadian tonnes.
Sanctions Relief Restores Belarusian Supply to US Market
A 30,000-tonne cargo of Belarusian MOP is scheduled to discharge in New Orleans on October 14, marking the first US-bound Belarusian potash shipment in four years. The Belarusian Potash Company loaded the cargo at Russia’s port of Bronka. The World Bank MOP benchmark fell for a third consecutive month to $367.50 per tonne in September from $405.00 in May, increasing price pressure as Belarusian supply returns.
The 30,000-tonne cargo equals about 0.5% of 2025 US potash imports, limiting its immediate market impact. US potash imports reached 5.6 million tonnes of potassium oxide equivalent in 2025, with net import reliance at 92%. The larger shift is the reopening of a supply channel that carried 635,000 tonnes a year before the 2021 designations.
Lost Klaipeda Access Raises Potash Delivery Costs Through Russia
Before the 2021 designations, Lithuania’s Klaipeda terminal handled 9 million to 11 million tonnes of Belarusian potash a year. With Klaipeda closed to Belarusian cargo, shipments now move by rail through Russia to Baltic ports such as Bronka, adding transport and handling costs. Arif Gasilov, partner at Gasilov Group, said Belarus moved 11.6 million tonnes through Russian ports in 2025. Higher rail, port, insurance and handling costs reduce the competitiveness of Belarusian potash in the US, limiting the pricing threat to Canadian supply.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License 13 covering Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company in December 2025 and delisted both in March 2026 after Belarus released about 250 political prisoners, reopening US trade with the companies. The EU has not matched the US relief, leaving Belarusian potash subject to EU restrictions and limiting its access to European buyers.
Committed Volumes Limit Near-Term Price Pressure
Existing sales contracts currently limit additional Belarusian potash supply to Western markets, with President Alexander Lukashenko saying Belarus has no uncommitted volumes available. Josh Linville, Vice President of Fertilizer at StoneX, noted that US buyers have had no difficulty sourcing potash, while phosphate and nitrogen remain the tighter nutrients.
Returning Supply Pressures Margins More Than Sales Volumes
For Saskatchewan-focused potash producers, returning Belarusian supply threatens realized prices more than sales volumes. Nutrien’s February 18, 2026 guidance estimates that each $25 per tonne change in potash net selling prices corresponds to $280 million of adjusted EBITDA and $0.45 of adjusted earnings per share. With tonnes already placed, additional New Orleans supply would pressure realized prices rather than displace sales volumes.
Producers with export logistics can redirect tonnes offshore, reducing exposure to weaker regional pricing. That flexibility can protect sales volumes when domestic supply increases. A pre-production developer without offtake remains exposed to benchmark prices when production begins.
No program volume or delivered price has been published, leaving the scale of Belarusian supply and its price impact uncertain, while the US Treasury retains the ability to restore sanctions. For Saskatchewan-focused producers, the key risk remains margin pressure from lower realized potash prices rather than the volume of a single cargo. For pre-production projects underwritten above $400 per tonne, a $365 benchmark can weaken projected returns and financing economics.
What Cost Position Supports Potash Returns
US sanctions restricted Belarusian potash supply, while their removal is reopening that trade channel. The World Bank MOP benchmark began falling three months before the Belarusian cargo was due, indicating the price decline preceded its return.
Since 2022, Saskatchewan-focused producers have benefited more from stronger netbacks than higher volumes, making realized pricing a key valuation driver. US Geological Survey (USGS) projects global potash capacity at 77.4 million tonnes of potassium oxide equivalent by 2029 versus 45.3 million tonnes of consumption, making delivered cost increasingly important to project economics.
Long-term value depends on delivered cost. Lower prices can delay higher-cost projects, favoring producers that remain competitive at lower potash prices. Saskatchewan producers can rail potash directly into the US Midwest, while Belarusian supply requires additional rail, port, insurance and handling costs through Russia.

high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Cluster: 6.3GW Power and Water Supply Key to 2030 Mass Production  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are accelerating the Honam Semiconductor Cluster, a project with total investment exceeding 800 trillion won (approximately $595.8 billion), targeting first mass production by 2030. Whether power and water infrastructure can be secured in time has emerged as the key variable determining the project's success or failure.
Around 20 officials from the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City's semiconductor industry support division and related bureaus visited Samsung Electronics' Pyeongtaek Campus on the 6th. This marks their second visit, following one on July 29. The delegation toured fabs and utility facilities within the Pyeongtaek Campus to examine semiconductor production processes and power and water supply systems, and planned to hear investment-related opinions and recommendations from Samsung Electronics.
They subsequently visited Pyeongtaek City Hall to review the administrative framework that simultaneously supports land, power, water, transportation, and logistics required for semiconductor plants. In the afternoon, they toured the Godeok International New Town and Brain City to inspect residential hinterland and commuting conditions.
The Pyeongtaek Campus currently operates four fabs, with a fifth fab, P5, under construction. Samsung Electronics is rushing to expand Pyeongtaek in response to growing demand for AI memory while simultaneously investing in the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex. The integrated city's return visit to Pyeongtaek is aimed at directly observing how a region already equipped with large-scale production facilities and infrastructure operates.
2030 Mass Production Target: Power and Water Are the Key
The Honam Semiconductor Cluster is a project to build a production hub of four fabs on the former Gwangju Military Airport site, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix investing a combined total of over 800 trillion won. The Korea Land & Housing Corporation (LH) is currently conducting survey and design services for the national industrial complex. The total site spans approximately 2.5 million pyeong, with plans to prioritize development of approximately 630,000 pyeong.
The South Korean government and the integrated city aim to begin groundwork on the priority development site as early as next year and commence first mass production by mid-2030. Discussions with SK Hynix are ongoing. The integrated city plans to sign a move-in agreement with SK Hynix this month, followed by negotiations on detailed investment conditions including land, construction, power, and water.
To meet the 2030 mass production target, power and water supply networks must be established before fab construction. Full operation of four fabs is estimated to require approximately 6.3 gigawatts (GW) of power. Initially, existing substations and power grids will be utilized, with plans to add transmission lines and substation facilities as production capacity expands.
Industrial water demand is projected at up to 650,000 tons per day. Semiconductor production requires massive volumes of ultrapure water for wafer cleaning and other processes, meaning water source development and pipeline construction must align with fab operation timelines.
The integrated city's plan calls for supplying an initial 3.1GW of power, scaling up to approximately 6.3GW as production facilities expand, and securing 150,000 tons of daily water supply by the end of 2028 before expanding supply capacity in phases.
The following table summarizes the core infrastructure demand and supply plans for the Honam cluster:
| Category | Final Demand | Initial Supply Target | Notes | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Power | Approx. 6.3GW | 3.1GW | Phased expansion aligned with production facility growth | 
| Industrial Water | Up to 650,000 tons/day | 150,000 tons/day by end of 2028 | Water source development and pipeline construction in parallel | 
In August, the South Korean government pushed for exemptions from preliminary feasibility studies for related projects to accelerate power and water infrastructure development for the Honam Semiconductor Cluster. The Korea Semiconductor Industry Association also stated in a position paper on August 11 regarding the implementation of the Special Semiconductor Act: "It is of paramount importance that investment support, core infrastructure development including power and water, and follow-up support policies are pursued swiftly and consistently."
Comparison with Pyeongtaek and Yongin: Infrastructure Determines Operational Timing
In Pyeongtaek and Yongin as well, power and water are the critical conditions determining fab operational timing. Pyeongtaek already has transmission networks, water pipelines, roads, and a supplier base in place, enabling Samsung Electronics to rapidly proceed with follow-up investments such as P5.
By contrast, the Yongin Idong-Namsa National Industrial Complex, where Samsung Electronics will be located, requires not only land compensation and site preparation but also simultaneous construction of transmission and water networks. Even if production facility construction proceeds quickly, actual operational timing can be delayed if infrastructure lags behind.
SK Hynix is likewise building its first fab at the Yongin Wonsam-myeon semiconductor cluster while continuing investments in its Cheongju production facilities. Once Honam investment begins in earnest, the company will be undertaking large-scale investments simultaneously in Yongin, Cheongju, and Honam.
Industry observers view the ability to supply power and water when actually needed as the more critical factor for the Honam cluster. With demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI growing rapidly, any misalignment between production facility and infrastructure construction schedules could delay mass production timing.
Combining Gwangju's Land with Jeonnam's Infrastructure
The Honam Semiconductor Cluster is a project that combines Gwangju's industrial base and land with Jeonnam's power, water, and renewable energy infrastructure resources. Before integration, Gwangju's industrial land and corporate support policies and Jeonnam's power generation facilities, water resources, and renewable energy had to be coordinated between separate local governments. Now, a single integrated city can bundle these elements and present them as investment conditions to companies while coordinating the project.
The integrated city is not limiting its ambitions to attracting semiconductor plants. It plans to expand into AI, renewable energy, data centers, and materials, components, and equipment industries, linking the South Korean government's maximum integrated support of 20 trillion won (approximately $14.9 billion) and the second phase of public institution relocation to build a super-regional industrial ecosystem.
On the fiscal front, the integrated city has decided to allocate 6 trillion won (approximately $4.5 billion) of the maximum 20 trillion won in fiscal incentives secured through integration toward semiconductor infrastructure, forward and backward industrial ecosystems, and specialized workforce development from 2027 to 2030.
Semiconductor investment has also provided new momentum for the long-stalled relocation of Gwangju Military Airport. Since the military airport site must be vacated for semiconductor production facilities to be built on schedule, the airport relocation has become linked to national advanced industry investment timelines, transcending its status as a long-standing regional issue. The South Korean government is also pursuing temporary dispersal of military functions and relocation procedures in parallel with fab groundbreaking.
Plans are also underway to attract materials, components, and equipment companies centered on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and to connect Gwangju's existing back-end processing base, including Amkor Technology Korea, to concentrate the semiconductor forward and backward industries in the region. By linking the national AI computing center at Haenam Solar City, private data centers, and Jeonnam's renewable energy production base, the project could expand into a super-regional industrial axis spanning semiconductor production, back-end processing, AI, and energy.
However, challenges remain: the industrial complex development, military airport relocation, and power and water supply networks must all be built on schedules aligned with corporate timelines, and the benefits of semiconductor investment must be spread beyond the Gwangju Military Airport area to industries and jobs across the entire Jeonnam-Gwangju region.

high_priority_articles.title: Piero Cipollone: Money in the digital age: digital euro, tokenisation and the role of central banks
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
Money in the digital age: digital euro, tokenisation and the role of central banks
Speech by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, MNI Connect Webcast
Frankfurt am Main, 6 October 2026
For centuries, issuing money and safeguarding its value has been at the heart of central banks’ mandate.
But the technological environment is changing.
People increasingly pay digitally. Financial institutions are experimenting with distributed ledger technology (DLT). Assets are being represented as digital files, or tokens. New actors have entered markets traditionally served by banks.
This transformation opens up significant opportunities.
It can make payments more convenient and finance more efficient. And it can pave the way for new products and business models.
But it also creates risks.
If we do not provide a digital form of cash, the role of public money may continue to decline. And we may find ourselves trapped in a situation where there is no pan-European digital payment solution that caters to every type of day-to-day transaction.
If tokenised finance develops on closed, incompatible platforms without a safe settlement asset, fragmentation could increase and the singleness of money could be weakened.
And when Europe depends excessively on infrastructures, technologies or solutions controlled elsewhere, our resilience and monetary sovereignty is diminished.
The question, therefore, is not whether payments and finance will become more digital. They already are.
The question is how we can ensure that our monetary system continues to preserve the singleness of money, trust and stability, while also supporting efficiency, resilience and autonomy as this transformation unfolds.
Our answer is to extend central bank money into the digital environment while preserving the two-tier monetary system in which public and private money coexist.
In retail payments, this means preparing for a digital euro. In wholesale markets, it means ensuring that central bank money can be used to settle tokenised transactions – through Pontes – while working with the market – through Appia – to shape the wider digital finance ecosystem.
These initiatives are often discussed separately. But they are all part of one comprehensive strategy: to keep central bank money at the heart of retail and wholesale finance, while giving European market participants the infrastructure they need to innovate, grow and remain competitive internationally.
Central bank money as the anchor
Our monetary system rests on the coexistence of public and private money.
Central bank money is the ultimate risk-free settlement asset. And it supports the role of private money because trust in commercial bank money rests on its convertibility at par into central bank money.
This convertibility ensures the singleness of money. One euro has the same value as any other, throughout the euro area.
Our objective is not therefore to replace private money or private innovation. It is to provide a stable public foundation to ensure day-to-day payments are cheap, resilient and inclusive. And to enable financial innovation to develop safely, at scale, in an integrated European market.
Preparing a digital euro for retail payments
Let me turn first to retail payments. This is what the digital euro is for: our day-to-day transactions.
A Europe-made, Europe-wide payments solution
There is still no European digital means of payment that works across all euro area countries and all major use cases.
European private solutions tend to cover specific markets or payment situations. This means that banks and their customers depend heavily on international card schemes and global technology companies.
Two-thirds of euro area card payments rely on international schemes. Of the 21 euro area countries, 13 have no domestic card scheme. And where a domestic payment solution exists, it does not always cater to all use cases and cannot be used in other euro area countries without co-badging with international schemes.
This is not just a question of sovereignty, resilience and freedom of choice. It is also a question of competitiveness.
European payment service providers have so far been unable to compete with international payment solutions on a European scale, let alone at global level. This is mainly because it would be costly for each individual provider to develop a Europe-wide acceptance network.
The recent announcement of an interoperability platform that would allow private payment solutions to share customers, enabling users to pay wherever interoperable solutions are accepted, is a step in the right direction and one we very much welcome. But much remains to be done: cross-border transactions account for just 5% of the market and interoperability does not expand acceptance domestically, nor does it broaden the use cases covered.
The digital euro would fill this gap.
It would provide a digital form of central bank money for everyday payments, complementing cash and private solutions. It would be available both online and offline and would be usable throughout the euro area for most use cases: person-to-person payments, e-commerce transactions and payments in physical shops.
But the ECB would not provide customer-facing services. Banks and other regulated payment service providers would distribute the digital euro, manage customer relationships and develop complementary services.
Our objective is not to take over the role of banks. On the contrary, the digital euro would equip banks with the infrastructure they need to compete in the digital age and help them expand the reach and use cases of their own solutions.
A platform payment service providers can build on
The digital euro would provide a common acceptance layer across the euro area.
Its legal tender status would give it pan-European reach: it would be accepted wherever digital payments can be made.
The digital euro’s open standards could be used by private payment services providers, thereby simplifying acceptance at physical points of sale, online and in mobile commerce.
The ECB has signed agreements with the European Card Payment Cooperation, nexo standards and the Berlin Group to reuse established European technical standards for digital euro payments. This should minimise adoption costs.
Co-badging would add to these benefits. Banks could integrate the digital euro into existing cards or mobile applications alongside their own payment solutions. Where a private solution is accepted, it could remain the preferred option. Where coverage is incomplete, the digital euro would step in to ensure that private solution users can still pay.
A sustainable economic model
The digital euro is also being designed with a sustainable economic model in mind.
The Eurosystem would bear the costs of establishing and operating its core infrastructure and would not charge any scheme or processing fees for digital euro transactions. Banks and payment service providers would be compensated for the services they provide. The precise arrangements are currently being discussed as part of the legislative process.
The digital euro is not therefore simply a new public payment instrument. It would provide public infrastructure that can help private European solutions scale up, offer value-added services and compete more effectively Europe-wide.
Safeguarding financial stability
Whenever a central bank proposes a digital form of money, a legitimate question arises: could deposits leave banks, impairing their capacity to provide credit?
We have taken this question very seriously.
The digital euro is being designed as a means of payment, not an investment product. It would not be remunerated, and individual holdings would be subject to limits.
Users would be able to link their digital euro holdings to a commercial bank account. A waterfall mechanism would allow users to make payments exceeding their digital euro balance by drawing the difference from that account. A reverse-waterfall mechanism could be used to automatically transfer to the linked bank account incoming amounts above the holding limit – or an even lower threshold if the customer so wishes. Behavioural research suggests that this approach could drive up digital euro adoption while reducing individual holdings.[1]
The limits will have to be calibrated to balance three objectives: making the digital euro convenient to use, safeguarding financial stability and preserving the smooth implementation and transmission of monetary policy.
Detailed analysis supports these safeguards.[2]
At the request of the European Parliament, the ECB examined the possible effects of hypothetical holding limits from €500 to €3,000 on the balance sheets of 2,025 banks, including both significant and less significant institutions.
It considered two scenarios: business-as-usual and flight-to-safety. The flight-to-safety scenario is an extreme tail scenario that has not occurred over the first 25 years of the euro. It also assumes no monetary policy response, although a crisis of this sort would normally lead the central bank to consider taking action.
The results are reassuring under both scenarios.
Under the business-as-usual scenario the introduction of the digital euro is projected to have an extremely contained impact on banks’ liquidity and funding metrics.
Indeed, digitalisation itself supports bank deposits, as payments migrate from cash to deposit-based instruments. Our analysis estimates a potential €127 billion deposit inflow by 2034, equivalent to 0.4% of banking sector assets or 1.5% of retail sight deposits. At aggregate level, this exceeds the estimated digital euro-related outflows in the business-as-usual scenario for holding limits up to and including €3,000. No aggregate outflow would thus be recorded.[3]
If we disregard the deposit inflows resulting from the continuing decline in the use of cash, the aggregate liquidity coverage ratio would fall only slightly, from 166% to 163%, for a limit

high_priority_articles.summary: Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he champions diplomacy and downplays differences  AP NewsIn Iceland, Rubio Dodges a Diplomatic Flap Over a Trump Map  The New York TimesSecretary of State Marco Rubio And Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir At a Joint Press Availability  U.S. Department of State (.gov)Rubio starts European tour in Iceland to boost security ties  Al JazeeraRubio begins three-nation NATO tour in Iceland, which ...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
REYKJAVIK, Iceland (AP) — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to reassure NATO ally Iceland that President Donald Trump’s administration has no designs on the island but shares its deep concerns about Arctic security as tensions between the United States and Russia rise in the High North and elsewhere.
Rubio hailed the role of diplomacy in resolving conflicts as he began a three-nation tour of NATO allies in the capital of Iceland, where concerns over the Republican administration’s often brusque and sometimes rude approach to traditional friends and partners have stirred unease.
Rubio, whose stops also include Greece and Portugal, met Tuesday with Iceland’s minister for foreign affairs, Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, at Reykjavik’s Hofdi House, the site of the 1986 summit between U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev that is widely regarded as the beginning of the end of the Cold War.
“The house symbolizes diplomacy’s role in ending the Cold War and defeating communism,” Rubio posted on social media after the talks that took place just days before the 40th anniversary of the landmark meeting.
Both Rubio and Gunnarsdóttir downplayed differences and said both countries were committed to deepening and expanding military and commercial ties. Rubio made clear that the United States would not do anything in Iceland without Iceland’s consent.
“We would be open to having those conversations to see what we can do together,” he said, noting that the U.S. had a decades-long permanent military presence in Iceland until 2006, when shifting priorities caused it to close its Keflavik base outside of Reykjavik. He noted that priorities have shifted again.
And he went out of his way to praise Iceland: “We have tremendous respect for the people. We have respect for the country in the role it plays, and it has for a very long time,” he said.
Iceland’s foreign minister says she’s ‘focused on the future’
Iceland has been uneasy about Trump’s intentions toward it after he posted a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and extending to Iceland and Greenland. The wariness has persisted despite an agreement last month to increase the U.S. presence in the neighboring Danish territory of Greenland that appears to have ended Trump’s earlier demand for the U.S. to take full control.
But Tuesday, after Rubio’s talks with Gunnarsdóttir and Iceland Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, those tensions appeared to be on the wane.
Gunnarsdóttir said the matter had been largely, if not entirely, resolved. “We remain focused on the future,” she said.
Rubio, meanwhile, said he was not in Iceland to talk about social media posts. “Everything is very positive,” he said.
Rubio said Monday that the visit was intended to “advance our shared priorities: a secure Arctic, stronger commercial and energy ties, and closer defense cooperation.” He offered no hint of tensions with the island that, while a NATO member, has no standing army.
The map incident, however, alarmed Icelanders, and in response, Gunnarsdóttir summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long to a meeting at which she made it clear the post was unacceptable.
Iceland, which is just 180 miles (290 kilometers) from Greenland, had already been on edge after Trump mistakenly named the country four times while speaking about Greenland.
Thousands of Icelanders signed a petition urging the prime minister to reject Long before he took up his ambassador post in August after he made a crack this year about Iceland becoming the 52nd U.S. state and making him governor. He has since apologized for the quip.
US ambassador to Greece faces misconduct allegations
At Rubio’s next stop in Athens, he may be dealing with another ambassador controversy. Rep. Gregory Meeks, a New York Democrat who is the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said he would investigate allegations of misconduct and impropriety by the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle.
In a letter to Rubio, Meeks said that he wanted answers following the allegations reported by The Wall Street Journal last month and that he would call for Guilfoyle’s dismissal if the behavior outlined in the news report were true.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Some Greek opposition parties have called for an inquiry into the allegations, but it’s unclear if they will proceed.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing, and Rubio has defended her before.
Guilfoyle, Rubio said after the Journal story appeared, “has been an incredible advocate for the president’s agenda in Greece and across Europe.” Rubio said he and Trump greatly value the ambassador’s “pivotal work and leadership,” notably on energy issues.
The Trump administration sees Greece as key to advancing the promotion and export of U.S.-produced liquefied natural gas to Southeastern and Central Europe.
Outside parliament on Tuesday, about 1,500 people gathered to protest Rubio’s visit and the war in Iran, chanting “American killers!”
The demonstration, organized by a communist labor union and other left-wing groups, was held ahead of extensive road closures planned in Athens on Wednesday.
Organizers said protests were held in at least 12 other Greek cities.
